tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Motions > Christmas Felicitations > Mr NATHAN HAGARTY
tree_branches.text:
Mr NATHAN HAGARTY ( Leppington ) ( 18:34 :48 ): Earlier this year I informed the House about the collapse of First Guardian Master Fund. It was marketed as a high-growth super investment but resulted in severe losses. It was then believed some 6,000 investors, including some from Leppington, and up to $600 million was affected. It can now be revealed that the scale of this disaster has practically doubled. According to the latest information revealed by the Australian Securities and Investment Commission, or ASIC, more than 11,000 Australians have now been caught up in the collapse of the First Guardian and Shield master funds, with over $1.2 billion in retirement savings potentially lost. What began as a major concern has now grown into one of the most significant superannuation failures in our nation's history.

In recent months, ASIC has launched significant enforcement action in response to what it described as "industrial‑scale misconduct". It has launched action against InterPrac Financial Planning for failing to ensure its representatives act in its clients' best interests and for facilitating more than $600 million in super investments in First Guardian and Shield. It has launched action against Ferras Merhi for allegedly directing clients into these schemes, while receiving almost $40 million in fees, commissions and marketing payments. It has also taken action against SQM Research for allegedly issuing favourable ratings of high-risk products in ways that ASIC says misled consumers.

These actions, some of which ASIC has described as "first of their kind", highlight the scale of systemic failure and the growing scrutiny of the broader network of financial actors that enabled these funds to reach mainstream superannuation platforms. One of the most serious issues is how easily First Guardian and Shield were able to appear on major superannuation platforms, including Macquarie Wrap, Netwealth, OneVue and AMP's North. The inclusion of these funds on mainstream platforms gave them the perception of credibility and drove inflows from advisers and consumers alike. Macquarie, under regulatory pressure from ASIC, has agreed to fully reimburse Shield investors on its platform. That is a $321 million commitment.

Other platforms should seriously consider following Macquarie's lead. The scandal is not the fault of one government, regulator or era. It has been decades in the making under multiple regulatory regimes. The deeper problem is structural. The industry is riddled with inherent conflicts. Funds rely on platforms to distribute products, platforms rely on advisers to drive inflows, and advisers rely on commissions and incentives. All of these depend on research houses, which are paid by the very funds they are meant to assess. Every link in the chain is conflicted, and those conflicts ultimately left consumers last.

Victims and advocacy groups have been very clear about their demands. They want to see an expansion and strengthening of the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort so that victims have access to redress. They want to see the adoption of a pay now, recover later model, as used in the HIH collapse and the National Redress Scheme, whereby government compensates the victims upfront and then recovers funds from those responsible—the trustees, licensees, product issuers, research houses and potentially their directors. They want to see the strengthening of governance and accountability by enforcing platform and trustee transparency, holding research houses to account, and banning conflicted remuneration for high-risk products.

Finally, they would like to see a full parliamentary inquiry. I also called for that earlier this year when I spoke about this issue. We must examine how First Guardian and Shield bypassed oversight, how they accessed major platforms, how trustee and research house scrutiny failed, how hundreds of millions of dollars were moved offshore, and how this conduct escaped ASIC, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority and the Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre despite repeated red flags.

At the centre of that scandal are everyday Australians who did nothing wrong. They are teachers, retail workers, carers and tradespeople who entrusted their futures to a system that promised security. Instead, their savings were used to buy sports cars and fund lavish lifestyles and were channelled offshore, far from the reach of ordinary Australians. The only just outcome is for most, if not all, of those victims' funds to be recovered. They were let down by a system that claimed to safeguard them. It is now that system's responsibility to deliver justice, reform and accountability.

tree_branches.name: Mr ADAM CROUCH
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Motions > Christmas Felicitations > Mr ADAM CROUCH
tree_branches.text:
Mr ADAM CROUCH ( Terrigal ) ( 14:37 :43 ): I am delighted to deliver my felicitation speech as the Opposition Whip. I start out by thanking the Speaker, his incredible office and staff; you, Madam Temporary Speaker; and all those on the Speaker's Panel. I acknowledge all Government members, including the Whip. Colleen needs to start writing his speeches so that he can finish on time. I acknowledge the Leader of the House and all of his team. Omar does a great job holding the place together as well. I take the opportunity to thank the Leader of the Opposition, the Hon. Mark Speakman. You would not find a harder working person in this place than he, who does a truly outstanding job. It is an honour and a privilege to be the Opposition Whip and a shadow Minister under his leadership. His incredible office is run by his truly outstanding chief of staff, Cheryl Gwilliam, and the team.

My good mate Richie Williamson, The Nationals Whip, is in the Chamber. Richie and I were talking today, saying that we make a great team. It is an absolute joy and pleasure to work with Rich. He is a wonderful person to work with. I also give a shout out to the Government Whip and the Deputy Government Whip, Liesl Tesch, who just entered the Chamber. I also give a shout out to Colleen Symington. Let's be clear: Colleen runs the place. Colleen, you are not allowed to go away or leave early, because every time you do, this place falls apart. I also acknowledge the incredible work done by the previous Whip's adviser, Bo Ok. She will be greatly missed. I look forward to catching up with Bo over Christmas. Welcome to Anthony Radic, who is doing a truly outstanding job with those big shoes to fill. It is a big job, and he is doing it incredibly well. Thanks, Anthony, for looking after all of us.

I also thank all of the team in here that do what they do every single day to make us look better, whether it be the incredible Hansard team behind me, the truly amazing Clerks in this place, led by the incredible Helen Minnican, with Carly and our Serjeant-at-Arms, Simon. I thank all of the Legislative Assembly attendants who keep this place running, including by putting the air conditioning temperature down at question time for me, because it gets very warm in here with 93 people all trying to talk at the same time. I often start a contribution by saying, "I will make a brief contribution", which means I will always go over time, but I will try and stay on message today.

I acknowledge all of my colleagues in the Opposition, both Liberals and Nationals, for the great work that they do for their electorates every single day, especially in this place—a lot of them travel a long way, like my friend Richie Williamson, and are away from their families for long periods—because we are proud and privileged to do what we do in this place. I acknowledge Gurmesh Singh, the new Leader of The Nationals, and the former Leader of The Nationals, Dugald Saunders. I acknowledge the whole leadership team in the Liberal Opposition. They do an incredible job.

I am really pleased that the member for Wyong is present in the Chamber. I thank him, too, for his friendship and camaraderie in what has been a pretty tough year and a half for me. I greatly respect the work that he does. I know how tough it is being in government. I will keep saying to him: "Be an irritant and go for every single dollar." He knows exactly what I mean by that. The member for Wyong is a great representative of the Central Coast—it is a pleasure working with him—as is the member for Gosford.

Mr David Harris: We share views on council.

Mr ADAM CROUCH: Absolutely. I have a deep sense of gratitude to the truly amazing people of the Terrigal electorate. It is a privilege and an honour to represent them and be the voice for our community in this Parliament. I thank them, as their elected representative, for the continued support they have provided me, and for their genuine caring, which means everything to me. They know what that means. Not a day goes by where someone does not ask how I am going. I am very privileged to have 55,000 support workers, and I am very lucky to represent them. They are a truly incredible group of people. It is an awesome responsibility and privilege, which I love doing, every single day.

I thank my incredible electoral office—Jack Robinson, Donna Golightly, Julie McFadden, Debra Beattie and Adam Walton—for doing the best job of looking after a wonderful group of people. I am so proud of what they do every single day. I boast that I have the best team anywhere. I know everyone says that, and we do. We are so lucky to have great electoral office staff who spend so much time caring for the people that we represent. Obviously they take their jobs very seriously. I hope they have a well-earned Christmas break. In general, I wish everybody here a very merry Christmas, and a safe, prosperous and happy holiday time. It is time to spend with family, to have a break and—for those of us from the Central Coast—appreciate that we live in the best region, in the best State, in the best country in the world. We are so lucky to be able to spend time in those electorates and at home with our family, our loved ones and our friends.

Ms Trish Doyle: Wrap it up.

Mr ADAM CROUCH: I hear the member for Blue Mountains. I have not gone anywhere near as far over my time as the member for Leppington did. I am also better dressed than him today. Again, I thank my electorate and the spectacular community of the Central Coast. Have a safe and merry Christmas. It would be remiss of me not to thank our incredible volunteer surf lifesavers for the 100,000-plus hours that they are going to put in on our beaches, keeping 1.2 million people safe again this season. They are true rockstars, and they do their job for free because they want to keep people safe. I thank the team at Surf Life Saving Central Coast and my seven Surf Life Saving clubs for all the hard work they are going to do this season. We know that they go out there to keep everybody safe. Again, I wish everyone a very merry, safe and happy Christmas.

tree_branches.name: Ms LIESL TESCH
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Motions > Christmas Felicitations > Ms LIESL TESCH
tree_branches.text: Ms LIESL TESCH ( Gosford ) —Our 2025 Gosford Community Champion Award recipients have blown me away with their kindness, passion and generosity. I would like to acknowledge Lisa Caswell, an incredible woman who has ignited community spirit in many of us while showcasing kindness and bringing smiles to our vulnerable community members. Lisa has dedicated her time at Meals on Wheels Central Coast for several years to help our community members feel safe and independent and well fed. Being the kind spirit Lisa is, she always makes the clients happy when they received their meals from her. From the light-hearted chat to the caring actions, Lisa has provided more than just food because to some of these community members, seeing Lisa might be the best thing happened in their week. Meals on Wheels is an important organisation on the Central Coast and with people like Lisa, who have been modelling true community champion that make Meals on Wheels extra special to our community. I thank the fabulous Lisa Caswell for her compassion and kindness towards the Meals on Wheels community.

tree_branches.name: Mr RICHIE WILLIAMSON
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Motions > Christmas Felicitations > Mr RICHIE WILLIAMSON
tree_branches.text: Mr RICHIE WILLIAMSON ( Clarence ) —I would like to congratulate Benjamin Benn, who has recently celebrated a remarkable milestone of 25 years of employment with Casino Food Company. Benny's story is one of dedication, growth, and genuine Casino Food Company spirit. Benny's early days with the company started out on the processing floors before he spent some time as part of the customer service team. Benny quickly became known for his friendly nature and built exceptional rapport with both colleagues and customers. Today, Benny makes up part of the company's accounting team in Business Analysis. Benny's continued positive attitude and energy have seen him successful across all of his roles with Casino Food Company. His ability to connect with people and bring positivity to every interaction has shaped him into a standout presence throughout his journey at the business. Benny's dedication not only contributes to the success of Casino Food Company but also strengthens the broader business community through the example it sets, with milestones like this reminding us of the lasting value of loyalty, teamwork, and continuous personal growth. Congratulations Benny, on your 25 years and I wish you all the success in the years ahead.

tree_branches.name: Ms CHARISHMA KALIYANDA
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Motions > Christmas Felicitations > Ms CHARISHMA KALIYANDA
tree_branches.text: Ms CHARISHMA KALIYANDA ( Liverpool ) ( 16:36 :43 ): I recently had the pleasure of attending the open day hosted by the Australian Islamic Cultural Centre at Masjid Bilal—Bilal Mosque—in Hinchinbrook. This wonderful event created a welcoming space for people of all backgrounds from across the Liverpool community to visit the mosque, meet members of the local Muslim community and deepen their understanding of Islamic culture and traditions. Open days like this are vital in fostering mutual respect and strengthening community bonds. They highlight the important role that mosques play in our local area, not only as places of worship but also as hubs for learning, charity and connection. It was inspiring to see so many residents walk through the doors, engage in meaningful conversations and show genuine interest in the beliefs and practices of their neighbours. These moments of openness and curiosity make our community stronger and more inclusive. I extend my sincere thanks to the Australian Islamic Cultural Centre and the dedicated team at Masjid Bilal for their warm hospitality and for creating such an informative and welcoming day. Their efforts truly help bring our communities closer together.

tree_branches.name: Ms FELICITY WILSON
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Motions > Christmas Felicitations > Ms FELICITY WILSON
tree_branches.text: Ms FELICITY WILSON ( North Shore ) —I congratulate Middle Harbour Public School's Carnival for holding their Middle Harbour Public School Carnival. After a six-year hiatus, Middle Harbour Public School's P&C brought back the carnival, which is both a fundraiser and community event, and a must-attend event for all families and residents. Over 3,000 guests registered to attend, and the Carnival had a petting zoo, a giant slide, spinning tea cups, ponies and plenty of games for kids and adults to enjoy. There was great food on offer, including sausage sizzles and chips on a stick. There was also an assortment of craft goods and second-hand treasures to purchase. I acknowledge P&C President Dana Lightbody, Treasurer Andrea Voight, Secretary Carl Bunn and Committee Members Sarah Jarrett, Joanne De La Mar, and Carlotta Annan for their commitment and dedication, and for bringing back this iconic and well-loved event. I recognise Middle Harbour Public School Principal Laura Barry for her ongoing leadership and congratulate Middle Harbour Public School on their carnival.

tree_branches.name: Ms MARYANNE STUART
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Motions > Christmas Felicitations > Ms MARYANNE STUART
tree_branches.text:
Ms MARYANNE STUART ( Heathcote ) ( 15:10 :40 ): This is my first Christmas felicitations speech, even though it is my third Christmas in this place. As the member for Heathcote, covering regions from Kirrawee in the Sutherland shire to Bulli in the Wollongong local government area, I thank and acknowledge so many people who have made 2025 a successful year. I thank our teachers and school support staff them for caring for and teaching our young people. We have had a great year, with the turning of the sod on the new fit-for-purpose Sutherland Public School hall and the announcement of a fit-for-purpose hall for Heathcote High School. Both projects are long overdue. I thank the school communities, students and families for their advocacy and for working with me to deliver those fantastic pieces of infrastructure.

We have reopened Garie Road. I thank the Garie Surf Life Saving Club and the cabin communities for their patience. Their road was washed away three years ago, and the Minns Labor Government has delivered a new road, built back with resilience. I especially acknowledge the Garie Surf Life Saving Club, which has had a tough time maintaining its membership. I wish the club all the best for a strong 2026 and acknowledge the president, Brad Taylor, in particular. Heathcote Road was repaired—urgent work that needed to be carried out. I thank Transport for NSW for its work and the community for its patience. Work was completed on Bulli town centre to help address congestion and keep pedestrians, businesses and commuters safe. There were major works, repairs and upgrades on the T4 and South Coast train lines, which were especially needed after flooding and landslides in 2024. The work was required to ensure that everybody is kept safe. I again thank the Transport for NSW workforce. I thank the station staff who work on all of the train stations in my electorate, as well as the cleaners, who maintain everything beautifully.

I thank the Rural Fire Service volunteers, and their families and friends who support them. Those volunteers never stop training and maintaining their equipment. In particular, I thank Martin Surrey, commander of the NSW RFS Illawarra Sutherland Team. I also thank Brendon Neilly from the National Parks and Wildlife Service. Heathcote is home to the oldest national park in Australia. Brendon is the royal area manager of the Greater Sydney branch. I shout him out for everything he does to protect nature and that beautiful piece of landscape within that Heritage listed royal national park. Darian Brooker has become a dear friend. She is CEO of We, Future Leaders. I acknowledge her for facilitating our first high school resilience and leadership forum. Jeanne Zweck is the president of the Sutherland Shire Business Chamber. It is a pleasure to work with her to make sure the small business community is always heard. I thank our nurses and hospital staff at Bulli Hospital, Coledale Hospital and the Sutherland Hospital for their dedication to quality health care. I thank our police, Fire and Rescue and all 11 surf lifesaving clubs in Heathcote for everything they do. Whilst we are having fun on Christmas and New Year's Day, they will be keeping the community safe. I thank them for their ongoing work and volunteering.

I am on four parliamentary committees. I take the opportunity to thank all of the staff. We have had a big year travelling around with those committees. We have held a number of hearings, public forums and round tables. We literally just need to turn up to do our job because everything else is done by the secretariat staff. They hire venues, organise accommodation and arrange witnesses and organisations ahead of time. I thank the secretariat and Hansard staff for everything they do every day. I thank the library staff, Aboriginal liaison officers, sound crews and administrative staff. We could not do the job as well, or at all, without them.

I thank the amazing Colleen Symington in the Whip's office, and Omar for his calming influence and solid performance. I thank our wonderful leadership team—the Premier, the Deputy Premier and all our wonderful Ministers—for everything they do. They have amazing staff behind them who help us out. I thank all my colleagues, especially the class of 2023. I thank my office staff—Kerrie, Letitia, Kate, Ethan and Dan—for a fantastic year. I thank my beautiful family for keeping me grounded and supporting me. I still pinch myself that I represent the people of Heathcote in this place. I am blown away that I have the honour to serve them. I wish each and every one of them a safe and merry Christmas and a happy new year. I look forward to working with them for a bigger and better year in 2026 for everybody.

tree_branches.name: Ms JENNY LEONG
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Motions > Christmas Felicitations > Ms JENNY LEONG
tree_branches.text: Ms JENNY LEONG ( Newtown ) —On behalf of the Newtown electorate, I would like to congratulate the Camdenville P&C Association for their successful 2025 Community Building Partnership grant and thank them for their work supporting the Camdenville Public School learning community. The P&C will use this grant to complete improvements to the school's outdoor learning space by installing platforms, a wobble bridge, and a log ladder. These improvements will ensure all students have access to an inclusive and fun playground area. Outdoor learning areas are crucial in ensuring that young people have access to a healthy and well-rounded education, supporting them to be active as young people and throughout their lives. I thank the Camdenville P&C Association for them commitment to ensuring that young people in our community have access to fun and inclusive outdoor areas for learning and play and acknowledge their tireless efforts supporting teachers and young learners in our community.

tree_branches.name: Dr HUGH McDERMOTT
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Motions > Christmas Felicitations > Dr HUGH McDERMOTT
tree_branches.text:
Dr HUGH McDERMOTT ( Prospect ) ( 17:16 :06 ): I give my voice to a people whose history runs deeper than the rivers of Mesopotamia: the Chaldean‑Syriac‑Assyrian people of Iraq. For millennia they have carried the torch of civilisation. They are the inheritors of Babylon and Nineveh; guardians of law, literature and faith; and the keepers of one of the world's oldest languages—a dialect spoken by Christ. Yet in the modern era they have endured dispossession, displacement and denial—not for want of love for their homeland but because of the failure of others to recognise that the soil of Iraq belongs to all its children.

As the State member for Prospect, I have been fortunate to meet many remarkable multicultural organisations across our diverse Western Sydney community. Each of them plays an integral role, caring for individuals and maintaining and promoting culture. As their representative in Parliament, I have been proud to stand before this House to share their rich culture and help advocate for their communities. The Sydney chapter of the Assyrian Democratic Movement [ADM]—or Zowaa—is a leading example. Based in the Prospect electorate, the ADM is an active social and political organisation whose members strive to preserve and protect Assyrian culture. Their advocacy efforts strengthen our Assyrian‑Australian community in Western Sydney and in their traditional homelands, including the Nineveh Plains and the city of Mosul.

Recently I was pleased to meet with a delegation from the ADM's political bureau in Iraq, Ninab Yousif Toma and Ashur Slewa Nico. I thank Immanuel Sada and George Adam from the ADM Sydney chapter for introducing me to those great individuals. During our discussion, I was moved to hear of the ADM's fight for the democratic rights of its communities. For over four decades, its members have fought, through prison, persecution and martyrdom, for an Iraq that honours all its peoples without distinction. To this day, they are still fighting and advocating for national partnership. The ADM's story is etched with tragedy: the massacre at Simele in 1933, the destruction of Sorya in 1969, the terrors of the Ba'athist years and the darkness of ISIS. Yet through every storm, its members have persisted. Each epoch tested their endurance, but their advocacy remained steadfast and peaceful, born from spiritual strength and an abiding love for their homeland.

Today the ADM—in Western Sydney and at their bureau in Iraq—calls for partnership. The movement calls upon Iraq to fulfil the promise of its own constitution: to uphold Article 125 of the constitution, guaranteeing cultural, linguistic, and political rights; to amend laws that allow the forced Islamisation of minors; to reform the quota system that silences smaller voices; and to acknowledge, at last, the Chaldean‑Syriac‑Assyrian people as the original inhabitants of Iraq. The ADM requests that on 1 April the Babylonian and Assyrian New Year be designated a national holiday. Above all, the people seek to live alongside their compatriots in peace, with their minority rights respected and contributing, as they always have, to the progress and unity of Iraq. In a century that has too often forgotten the lessons of coexistence, the ADM's vision of partnership is a balm to the politics of division. It sends a clear message that diversity is not a threat; it is, in fact, a foundation.

The Assyrian Australian diaspora is strengthening the social, cultural and economic fabric of New South Wales. In suburbs like Smithfield, Fairfield, Wetherill Park, Prairiewood, Wakeley, Edensor Park and Bossley Park, our Assyrian community has built its roots, with churches like St Mary's Assyrian Church of the East and St Thomas The Apostle Chaldean Diocese to schools like St Narsai Assyrian Christian College and St Hurmizd Primary School. Our Assyrian Australian community are preserving their language, culture and faith whilst embracing the values, traditions and democratic freedoms of Australia. They are living proof that diversity, when respected, is a foundation for strength. This attests to their call for representation and parity in Iraq, calls which are echoed across the Prospect electorate. I am proud to stand in support of our Assyrian Australian community in the hope that one day their people will live freely and securely as respected owners of and equals in their ancestral homelands.

tree_branches.name: Mr DAVID LAYZELL
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Motions > Christmas Felicitations > Mr DAVID LAYZELL
tree_branches.text: Mr DAVID LAYZELL ( Upper Hunter ) —I want to acknowledge the ongoing work in the Upper Hunter to improve road safety starting with our newest road users. Upper Hunter Shire Council and Hunter Valley Police District began the Learner Night Driver Program in late-2024 and it is being strongly supported by the community. Hunter Learner Night Drive is for learner drivers of any age, who must be accompanied by an appropriately licenced supervisor aged over 25. The event exposes learner drivers to real life driving scenarios and the opportunity to interact with police in a controlled environment. Learner drivers use a track at Scone Airport and get to experience stationary and mobile breath tests with police as well as receiving advice and guidance on how to safely undertake these tasks. The track includes a section where drivers can practice reverse parallel parking, roadcraft and vehicle manoeuvring. Learner Night Drive is supported by Hunter Valley Highway Patrol, Transport for NSW, NSW Ambulance, Singleton Council, Muswellbrook Shire Council and Merriwa VRA. I also want to acknowledge the corporate supporters assisting this initiative including JBS Scone, Bengalla Mining Company, Pays Air Service and Hunter Warbirds.

tree_branches.name: Ms JANELLE SAFFIN
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Motions > Christmas Felicitations > Ms JANELLE SAFFIN
tree_branches.text: Ms JANELLE SAFFIN ( Lismore — Minister for Small Business, Minister for Recovery, and Minister for the North Coast ) —I WISH to congratulate Richmond Riverkeeper Kristin den Exter who was named winner of the Local Hero category at the 2025 NSW Coastal Conference Awards in Ballina recently. Kristin was recognised for her outstanding contribution to river health, community consultation, and coastal care. The award acknowledges Kristin's leadership through Richmond Riverkeeper and the Richmond RiverFest, a month-long celebration of culture, community and Country that connects people from the sea to the source. I have followed the work of the Richmond Riverkeepers closely and receive regular updates from them. Associate Professor in History at Southern Cross University and fellow Richmond Riverkeeper Adele Wessell told The Lismore App: "Kristen has been listening to what the river is telling us her whole life, listing to the knowledge of Custodians and First Peoples and committing herself to a lifetime of working with the river with integrity and love in a way that inspires everyone around her," Associate Professor Wessell said. For her part, Kristen spoke of collective effort: "From Elders and artists to scientists and volunteers, we're all working together so that the rivers of the Richmond catchment can one day be drinkable, swimmable and fishable again."

tree_branches.name: Ms ROBYN PRESTON
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Motions > Christmas Felicitations > Ms ROBYN PRESTON
tree_branches.text:
Ms ROBYN PRESTON ( Hawkesbury ) ( 17:31 :14 ): Merry Christmas to you, Mr Temporary Speaker.

TEMPORARY SPEAKER ( Mr Clayton Barr ): Merry Christmas to you too.

Ms ROBYN PRESTON: I speak about several momentous occasions that occurred recently within the Hawkesbury electorate. Known for its proud heritage and encompassing historic towns such as Windsor, St Albans, Richmond, Ebenezer and Wilberforce—to name a few—Hawkesbury is a special place to live in, visit and learn about. I am privileged to be the member for the electorate, and I thoroughly enjoy occasions when we reach and celebrate significant anniversaries and milestones in our community. This week the restored Thomas James Bridge was officially opened, and the event was an example of that great public pride and celebration. Located on Settlers Road at Wisemans Ferry, the bridge has played a crucial role in connecting regions of the Hawkesbury since its construction in 1830. The Thomas James Bridge holds the prestigious title of the oldest in‑use bridge on mainland Australia—a source of great pride for Hawkesbury communities.

Unfortunately, recent flooding severely compromised the area around the bridge, resulting in major landslips and impacting the safe use of the bridge for residents. Funding from the State and Federal governments' recovery program enabled reconstruction of the bridge, with local contractor Delaney Civil appointed to complete the project. I note that the member for Gosford is in the Chamber. She participated in the conversations that followed the tragedy on our shared boundary, as both councils reached out to us for support. Stages of preliminary site assessment, bridge reconstruction and adjacent rock face stabilisation were critical steps in achieving restoration of the site.

Admirably, huge efforts were made during the repairs. The 181 original sandstone blocks, quarried from the surrounding hillside in 1830 to build the bridge, were carefully removed from the site. The beautiful sandstone blocks, originally cut and moved by hand, were meticulously replaced in exactly the same position to honour and replicate the original bridge as much as possible. It is remarkable that it could be mirrored 195 years later. I was incredibly honoured to attend the reopening of the Thomas James Bridge and celebrate the efforts and achievements of the project. I congratulate contractors Civil Delaney, Hawkesbury City Council, Central Coast Council, Macdonald Valley Association and the community groups on their collaboration and perseverance in completing the project. A great sense of pride, accomplishment and connectedness to heritage was shared amongst attendees at the event.

On a similar note, I recently attended another momentous occasion in the Hawkesbury electorate. I joined students, staff and members of the community at Macdonald Valley Public School to acknowledge and celebrate the school's 180th anniversary. Current and former students came together to reflect on the school's long history and unique place in the heart of the valley. Carrying the distinction of being one of the oldest government schools in New South Wales, Macdonald Valley Public School inspires a strong sense of pride and connection among the students, which was very special to witness.

Principal Sarah Allen and the dedicated staff possess a clear passion for supporting their 13 students, ensuring their time at school is spent making strong friendships, partaking in meaningful learning engagements and connecting with the community. The celebration was a very special occasion that highlighted the projects and achievements of the students, who are clearly well supported, inspired and connected to their learning. I congratulate the students, staff and community of Macdonald Valley Public School on reaching that milestone, and I look forward to hearing about their future endeavours. I also recognise and congratulate Uncle Cole, who gave us a wonderful welcome to country and smoking ceremony on the day.

Our region continues to experience the pressures and pace of a changing world, but it is grounding to come together in moments that remind us of who we are, where we have come from and what binds our communities together. Those milestones highlight the strength that comes from honouring our heritage while looking confidently towards the future. Whether it is safeguarding our historic infrastructure or nurturing the next generation of learners, the Hawkesbury continues to show that progress and tradition are not opposing forces but partners in reshaping a thriving and connected community. I am deeply proud to represent an electorate where local history is cherished, community spirit is strong and our shared story continues to grow richer over time.

tree_branches.name: Mr JIHAD DIB
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Motions > Christmas Felicitations > Mr JIHAD DIB
tree_branches.text: Mr JIHAD DIB ( Bankstown — Minister for Customer Service and Digital Government, Minister for Emergency Services, and Minister for Youth Justice ) —I recently had the pleasure of attending the Wise Up: Empowering Youth and Community Program, proudly supported by the Campsie Police Area Command. This outstanding initiative focuses on helping young people build confidence and leadership skills through goal setting, teamwork, and personal development—empowering students to achieve their best both in and beyond the classroom. It was wonderful to meet and speak with students from Bankstown Girls High School and Unity Grammar, who shared their aspirations and the positive impact the program has had on their motivation and self‑belief. Their enthusiasm and determination were inspiring and a reflection of the program's success in fostering resilience and community connection among young people. A special thank you to Ali Faraj from the GWS Giants and Jamal Rifahi empowering, encouraging and reminding the students that with focus and perseverance, anything is possible. Gratitude also goes to our local NSW SES Canterbury Unit for generously providing their venue and ongoing support for youth engagement initiatives. Programs like Wise Up remind us of the importance of investing in our young people—empowering them to grow, lead, and contribute to a stronger, more connected community.

tree_branches.name: Dr JOE McGIRR
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Motions > Christmas Felicitations > Dr JOE McGIRR
tree_branches.text:
Dr JOE McGIRR ( Wagga Wagga ) ( 15:56 :54 ): It is a great privilege to make a contribution to Christmas felicitations. Our work in this place is, by its very nature, often adversarial. But I am heartened by the ideals that we all share and I am encouraged by our common purpose to do the best we can for our communities. Although we inevitably disagree, more often than not we find common ground in seeking the better future we all want for our electorates, our State and our nation. I am very fortunate to represent the people of the Wagga Wagga electorate. I thank my community for its optimism, can-do attitude and commitment to working together. I am proud of our achievements in 2025, not least the major progress on the Marshalls Creek Bridge, the start of a community emergency response team at the Rock, the opening of a new childcare centre at Lockhart, the progress on the Tolland Renewal Project and the opportunity to right a historic wrong in the upcoming Snowy Valleys Council demerger referendum. Those are just a few of my community's achievements.

I acknowledge and thank the Premier, Government Ministers and other Government members, as well as their staff, for responding to my advocacy and for the work they do. I also thank my crossbench colleagues for their collegiality and support. There is no doubt that the Legislative Assembly crossbench has been an effective enhancement to the lawmaking and government processes of this State. We may have different perspectives, but we share a passion for delivering a better future. I also acknowledge and thank members of the Opposition. It has been a privilege to work with members across all parties in this House to ensure that our communities have the best legislation. I thank the Leader of the House and his team, particularly Omar Rodriguez. I also acknowledge the Speaker and his staff, the Clerks and the staff of the Legislative Assembly. We are so fortunate to have their leadership and professionalism in the course of our duties.

I also thank Mark Webb and the Department of Parliamentary Services [DPS] staff for their great work and support—all the staff from cleaning and security, human resources and, of course, Hansard. This year, I particularly express my thanks to secretariats of the committees I have chaired. Special thanks to Rohan Tyler, Shaza Barbar, Carly McKenna, Emily Whittingstall, Reeti Pandharipande, Marcus Bell and Matt Johnson—I hope I have not left anyone out. It has been a busy year across the three committees that I chair. I have appreciated their hard work and professionalism, which have contributed so much to the outcomes that we have been able to achieve. I also thank my committee members.

More always needs to be done. At the top of my Christmas list is the duplication of Wagga Wagga's Gobbagombalin Bridge and the delivery of my six-point Rural Health Action Plan—a road map towards urgently needed reform to underpin the future of country communities across the State. The Government will hear more from me about these essential issues, amongst others. I am also mindful that there are people in my electorate and nearby who are dealing with the effects of drought. Having met with the Premier and Minister for Agriculture this week, and the mayors of Snowy Valleys Council and Greater Hume Shire Council, I will continue my advocacy on that issue. None of this would have been possible without the support of my staff and I would like to pay tribute to my team —Jennie Burns, Paul Terry, Rachelle Kell, Daniela Gooden, Jess Payne, Jess Masuda, Emma Mundy, Meg Mundy, Steph Plane, Fiona McPherson, Helen Foley and Lewis Pierotti. Their passion, dedication and hard work make my job easier and our community a better place.

Underpinning it all is my deep love for my family. My love and respect, as always, goes to my wife, Associate Professor Kerin Fielding, whose achievements as a surgeon and advocate for regional health are legendary. I thank her for her love and support. As many members have indicated, it is a tough gig in this House and the support of family is so important. Our children and their partners and children are a joy, and I express my love and gratitude to Lara and Duncan, Natasha, Dylan and Bel, and Anna. I am especially happy to welcome not only the engagement of Dylan and Bel but also to celebrate the arrival to the world of Lara and Duncan's second child, Hallie Wren Hellmers McGirr, little sister to our beloved first grandchild, Rachel. Thank you to all. I am proud of you all and love you very much,

Christmas is a time of celebration but for some it can be a time of loneliness and tension. I acknowledge that. On that note I also acknowledge the recent passing of my father-in-law, Professor Anthony Fielding, after a long illness. Anthony made an enormous contribution to our society and was a very important person in the lives of his daughters, Gail, Vickie and my wife Kerin. He was a very important person on our family. I offer my condolence to his widow, Margaret, and to his daughters and family. I pay my respects and pay tribute to Professor Anthony Fielding.

Christmas is the feast of when God became man. It is a time when we should enjoy the company of our loved ones. It is a season of hope for us all. We should all keep that in mind and celebrate the feast with a deep sense of gratitude for what we have, and a deep sense of hope for the future. From my family to yours, I wish everyone here a happy Christmas and a safe and prosperous new year. Thank you to all in this House for the work you do. I look forward to continuing our work together in 2025. Season's greetings and God bless, everyone.

tree_branches.name: Mr TIM JAMES
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Motions > Christmas Felicitations > Mr TIM JAMES
tree_branches.text: Mr TIM JAMES ( Willoughby ) —I congratulate Monalisa Jani, Teaching Director at CASS Gumnut Early Learning Centre in St Leonards, on receiving the Director/Nominated Supervisor Excellence Award at the 2025 Excellence in Early Childhood Education Awards. This honour reflects Monalisa's steady leadership, commitment to high standards and focus on each child's wellbeing and growth. Her work lifts outcomes for children and supports families through a caring and professional service. I acknowledge the whole CASS Gumnut team for their dedication to quality practice and continuous improvement. Strong partnerships with parents and carers are a hallmark of the centre and this award is a credit to that shared effort. Monalisa's achievement is a proud moment for St Leonards and the Lower North Shore and highlights the vital contribution of early childhood educators across our community. I'm proud of you Monalisa!

tree_branches.name: Ms STEPHANIE DI PASQUA
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Motions > Christmas Felicitations > Ms STEPHANIE DI PASQUA
tree_branches.text: Ms STEPHANIE DI PASQUA ( Drummoyne ) —I rise to acknowledge a local Rhodes resident and author, Dr Uma Srinivasan and to sincerely congratulate her on the launch of her new book 'Etched in Gold'. Etched in Gold is a historical fiction, telling the story of two Indian women connected through their passion for music and their culture throughout the 16th to 18th centuries. The novel is an important reminder of the power of storytelling in sharing histories and preserving cultural heritage. Prior to beginning her journey as an author, Dr Srinivasan worked as a computer scientist, obtaining her PhD from the University of New South Wales. Her transition to literature is a testament to her talent and dedication to lifelong learning. I have known Dr Srinivasan for a number of years during her time serving on the City of Canada Bay Council's Rhodes Community Committee, where she volunteered her time serving Rhodes and working to bring better services for the community. I sincerely congratulate Dr Srinivasan on the release of her novel 'Etched in Gold' and I wish her all the very best.

tree_branches.name: Mr STEVE WHAN
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Motions > Christmas Felicitations > Mr STEVE WHAN
tree_branches.text: Mr STEVE WHAN ( Monaro — Minister for Skills, TAFE and Tertiary Education ) —Last month, students from Delegate and Michelago Public Schools travelled to Sydney to compete at the NSW PSSA Athletics Championships. The PSSA is the pinnacle of public school sport in NSW and a great opportunity for young athletes from our country schools. I want to pay tribute to the principals of the schools, Mr Bannister from Delegate and Mr Smith from Michelago, who not only drove their students all the way to Sydney but also to Wollongong for the Regional Championships. Achievements like this truly show how small and regional public schools punch well above their weight – and they show the great commitment of our wonderful staff. Congratulations to all the students and teachers involved!

tree_branches.name: Mr NATHAN HAGARTY

tree_branches.text:
Mr NATHAN HAGARTY ( Leppington ) ( 18:34 :48 ): Earlier this year I informed the House about the collapse of First Guardian Master Fund. It was marketed as a high-growth super investment but resulted in severe losses. It was then believed some 6,000 investors, including some from Leppington, and up to $600 million was affected. It can now be revealed that the scale of this disaster has practically doubled. According to the latest information revealed by the Australian Securities and Investment Commission, or ASIC, more than 11,000 Australians have now been caught up in the collapse of the First Guardian and Shield master funds, with over $1.2 billion in retirement savings potentially lost. What began as a major concern has now grown into one of the most significant superannuation failures in our nation's history.

In recent months, ASIC has launched significant enforcement action in response to what it described as "industrial‑scale misconduct". It has launched action against InterPrac Financial Planning for failing to ensure its representatives act in its clients' best interests and for facilitating more than $600 million in super investments in First Guardian and Shield. It has launched action against Ferras Merhi for allegedly directing clients into these schemes, while receiving almost $40 million in fees, commissions and marketing payments. It has also taken action against SQM Research for allegedly issuing favourable ratings of high-risk products in ways that ASIC says misled consumers.

These actions, some of which ASIC has described as "first of their kind", highlight the scale of systemic failure and the growing scrutiny of the broader network of financial actors that enabled these funds to reach mainstream superannuation platforms. One of the most serious issues is how easily First Guardian and Shield were able to appear on major superannuation platforms, including Macquarie Wrap, Netwealth, OneVue and AMP's North. The inclusion of these funds on mainstream platforms gave them the perception of credibility and drove inflows from advisers and consumers alike. Macquarie, under regulatory pressure from ASIC, has agreed to fully reimburse Shield investors on its platform. That is a $321 million commitment.

Other platforms should seriously consider following Macquarie's lead. The scandal is not the fault of one government, regulator or era. It has been decades in the making under multiple regulatory regimes. The deeper problem is structural. The industry is riddled with inherent conflicts. Funds rely on platforms to distribute products, platforms rely on advisers to drive inflows, and advisers rely on commissions and incentives. All of these depend on research houses, which are paid by the very funds they are meant to assess. Every link in the chain is conflicted, and those conflicts ultimately left consumers last.

Victims and advocacy groups have been very clear about their demands. They want to see an expansion and strengthening of the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort so that victims have access to redress. They want to see the adoption of a pay now, recover later model, as used in the HIH collapse and the National Redress Scheme, whereby government compensates the victims upfront and then recovers funds from those responsible—the trustees, licensees, product issuers, research houses and potentially their directors. They want to see the strengthening of governance and accountability by enforcing platform and trustee transparency, holding research houses to account, and banning conflicted remuneration for high-risk products.

Finally, they would like to see a full parliamentary inquiry. I also called for that earlier this year when I spoke about this issue. We must examine how First Guardian and Shield bypassed oversight, how they accessed major platforms, how trustee and research house scrutiny failed, how hundreds of millions of dollars were moved offshore, and how this conduct escaped ASIC, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority and the Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre despite repeated red flags.

At the centre of that scandal are everyday Australians who did nothing wrong. They are teachers, retail workers, carers and tradespeople who entrusted their futures to a system that promised security. Instead, their savings were used to buy sports cars and fund lavish lifestyles and were channelled offshore, far from the reach of ordinary Australians. The only just outcome is for most, if not all, of those victims' funds to be recovered. They were let down by a system that claimed to safeguard them. It is now that system's responsibility to deliver justice, reform and accountability.

tree_branches.text: Ms LIZA BUTLER ( South Coast ) —I am delighted to recognise and celebrate the inspiring young artists whose work is now shining at the Shoalhaven Regional Gallery in Nowra. The latest exhibition showcases artwork created through the HOME Program, a powerful initiative inviting students from Falls Creek, Greenwell Point, Nowra, Sanctuary Point and Tomerong Public Schools to explore the meaning of 'home'. Over three school terms, these students connected deeply with local Aboriginal artists, community, language and culture. Guided by the talents of Aunty Cheryl Davison, Aunty Deidre Martin and cultural knowledge holder Allen Bloxsome, the students took part in workshops and virtual excursions that enriched their understanding and sparked their creativity. The HOME Program offers young people a meaningful opportunity to engage with First Nations stories, culture and history, building respect, understanding and a stronger connection to the land they call home. The artworks on display reflect this journey with honesty, depth and skill. I extend my heartfelt congratulations to every student artist, to the educators who supported them, and to the First Nations artists and partners who made this program possible. Mr MICHAEL REGAN ( Wakehurst ) ( 17:41 :35 ): Brookvale Public School is the fifth smallest school on the northern beaches, with around 310 students enrolled in 2025. However, it may be small in numbers but it is bursting with spirit. The tight‑knit school is a place of social connection, belonging and purpose. The dedicated staff nurture every child, supporting them to flourish. The school has a rich program of extracurricular activities and also supports academic excellence, hosting an opportunity class since the beginning of this year. The thriving school culture is testament to the commitment of all the teachers, mums and dad, and the great kids at the school. Tonight I acknowledge and thank the entire school community, particularly principal Mr Luke Richmond for his excellent leadership. Brookvale is one of many excellent public schools in my electorate of Wakehurst, but right now it is facing some unique pressures.

For over a year, the Brookvale P&C has raised legitimate concerns about high school catchment boundaries. Currently, Brookvale Public School falls in the catchment area for the Northern Beaches Secondary College Cromer Campus without access to local single sex school options. The department has said that will continue, even though the nearby Northern Beaches Secondary College Freshwater Senior Campus is transitioning to a comprehensive years 7 to 12 high school from 2027 and the new Forest High School is opening in Allambie Height, the suburb right next door. The clear request from the Brookvale P&C is to include Brookvale in the intake area for the new years 7 to 12 Freshwater campus. I am also keen to see maximum choice for Brookvale families, including opening up Forest High School, Mackellar Girls Campus and Balgowlah Boys' Campus.

There are several reasons why keeping Brookvale zoned to Cromer campus is illogical and including it in the Freshwater catchment makes a lot more sense. Firstly, is geographic accessibility: Freshwater campus will be the closest high school, just 1.4 kilometres away from Brookvale Public School. It is mostly flat and a walkable or rideable distance from home for many Brookvale students. Cromer campus is much further away, involving a longer and more complex commute of up to 45 minutes, including multiple bus transfers. Over six years of high school that is about 1,800 hours commuting, equivalent to almost a full school year spent just travelling.

Secondly, is about maintaining community connectedness. Listening to the parent body at Brookvale, the reality is their networks of sports and social activities are the same as the families who will attend the Freshwater campus. Brookvale children train and play with Brookvale Football Club in Manly, play netball at Curl Curl, or are members of Surf Life Saving clubs at Freshwater and Curl Curl, among countless other engagements. We need to encourage continuity and depth of social connection, for both parents and students, across different parts of their lives. Thirdly, and very importantly, there is a fairness, equity and inclusion dimension to this issue. The position statement from Brookvale P&C states:

The decision to exclude Brookvale from the Freshwater Campus intake also appears to deepen class-based inequalities in the Northern Beaches public school system. Brookvale is home to a far more diverse mix of ethnic, cultural, and socio-economic backgrounds than many surrounding suburbs. Yet, we are being cut off from the high school options being made available to wealthier areas like Freshwater, Curl Curl, Manly and Balgowlah.

Brookvale students and families should get the same choices and opportunities as surrounding suburbs. Brookvale is a small school, so we are talking about a low number of students each year, which will have minimal impact on numbers at the Freshwater campus. The Brookvale Public School community feels that, in both process and outcome, the current high school zoning decision is unjustified and unfair. Frankly, I agree with them. I will not go into the details, but I think the Department of Education could have been more responsive and transparent on this issue.

I thank the members of the P&C, particularly president Hina Osmany, for being so engaged, eloquent and persistent in their advocacy. Brookvale is a small school doing great things. It needs to be celebrated, maintained and supported, not undermined. I have made clear to the education Minister's office my strong view that Brookvale primary students should be zoned for Freshwater campus from day one in 2027. Depending on capacity, I also think Brookvale students should have the option of Forest High, Mackellar Girls or Balgowlah Boys. I have also sought and received the following commitments from the education Minister's office: firstly, for the education Minister to meet with the P&C leadership before the beginning of the 2026 school year; secondly, for an expression of interest survey process for students in years 4, 5 and 6 at Brookvale to get an accurate picture of their high school preferences and the numbers of students; and, thirdly, at the very least for there to be a catchment review in 2027, taking into account actual enrolments across all schools impacted by the zoning changes. However, I am pushing for this to happen in late 2026 so that, if possible, students can start at their preferred high school in 2027.

I have also requested that if Brookvale students are not included in the Freshwater campus catchment from day one in 2027, they should have formal out‑of‑area enrolment priority at Freshwater, Forest High, Mackellar Girls and Balgowlah Boys. I will continue to push for this and keep the community updated. School catchment boundaries may be lines on a map for the Department of Education, but for students and families these are life‑changing delineations. Decisions about school catchments need to be made with local insight and proper consultation. The wrong call has been made in this case, and I will keep pushing for a fairer, commonsense outcome for Brookvale families.

tree_branches.text: Ms DONNA DAVIS ( Parramatta ) —I was delighted to join the community on Saturday 1st November for Foundation Day, celebrating Parramatta's proud history and heritage. This year Foundation Day was held at Hambledon Cottage, providing an opportunity to introduce this State heritage listed site to a wider audience as families, friends and even a few four-legged locals enjoyed the free family event. Foundation Day marks the arrival of Governor Arthur Phillip in Parramatta on 2 November 1788 and the start of agricultural projects in the area. The date has traditionally been celebrated with large civic events, street carnivals and parades. In more recent years the actual day has become less of a focus than the sharing of Parramatta's heritage and stories. This year visitors enjoyed guided tours of Hambledon Cottage, horse drawn carriage rides, weaving and blacksmith demonstrations, roving entertainment, children's workshops, face painting an animal farm and entertainment from the Parramatta's City Band. Congratulations to the Parramatta and Districts Historical Society, the City of Parramatta, the Parramatta Lions Club and all who were involved in making the day a success.

Mr ROY BUTLER ( Barwon ) ( 18:44 :41 ): People in regional communities love a race—school sports carnivals, horses, greyhounds, trots, goats or even yabbies at a pub event. It is no different in Barwon. We do not have the same recreational and social opportunities that our metropolitan and coastal cousins have, and it is understandable that being at risk of losing something that is important to a community gets whole towns pretty fired up. Greyhound Racing NSW has the wrong mission or objectives as an organisation, and that needs to change. It has a commercial and financial focus, which has led to an announcement in the past couple of weeks of the intention to close 15 tracks that are all in regional New South Wales and are all non‑TAB tracks.

The objectives of Greyhound Racing NSW do not consider the social and cultural role that the sport plays in regional communities and the local economic impacts of its actions. It is more lost amenity and lost opportunity for social and family activity in regional New South Wales. The way the criteria were designed was always going to disadvantage regional and non-TAB track facilities. I believe that was intentional. The recommendations from Deloitte were predetermined by the criteria that were used.

My communities of Coonamble and Broken Hill have a strong and active group of greyhound enthusiasts. The rug was pulled from under their feet when they were told that they are being considered for closure in June 2026. Coonamble has experienced mixed messaging from Greyhound Racing NSW about its future, the annual Coonamble carnival and the works required to bring the track up to a standard that many other tracks still in use do not meet. Greyhound racing is an important part of the fabric of the Coonamble community, and the carnival is an important drawcard that drives people and money to Coonamble.

If the track at Broken Hill ceases to race, participants will go to Adelaide rather than New South Wales. The more they are on the road, the higher the chance of an accident. Dogs do not always do well after hours on the road in a trailer. I wonder if Greyhound Racing NSW has considered the welfare implications of making dogs travel. The criteria and weighting made it impossible to recommend Broken Hill continue because it has no surrounding communities within a 150-kilometre radius. It chooses not to race in the summer for welfare reasons. It is looking after the dogs.

Given the short time frame until closure in June, there is concern that no investment will be made in the last season. Many of the dogs would end up in the Greyhounds As Pets program. The design of the criteria and weighting system really set small clubs up to fail. Broken Hill has the infrastructure and the dogs, and the business is profitable. Broken Hill has never been told it is at risk and was given no option to negotiate. It is willing to make changes and accommodate changes. It has also been told previously that it is meeting or exceeding any benchmark it is required to.

I have heard examples of clubs that are banding together to offer support to other clubs. I would like to see that support from Greyhound Racing NSW. After 52 years as a club and 48 years as a non-TAB club, the last two years for Broken Hill have been spent contributing to the industry through TAB events. Under the current Greyhound Racing NSW approach, tracks like Broken Hill and Coonamble will be lost in regional areas. It is not just happening in Barwon. Tracks in Nowra, Tamworth, Maitland, Wentworth Park, Kempsey, Wagga Wagga, Young, Potts Park, Wauchope and Moree are all being considered for closure. The discussions I have had with greyhound trainers and racers suggest that it will certainly lead to people exiting the industry. They will not go to the trouble and expense of traveling for hours with dogs to other tracks.

What needs to happen? Any decision to close tracks needs to be put on hold pending a parliamentary inquiry into Greyhound Racing NSW and its actions. Scrutiny and accountability needs to be applied through the Parliament. The terms of reference for an inquiry should include the objectives of Greyhound Racing NSW and its suitability; equity of access to Greyhound Racing NSW funds for regional clubs; the support offered by Greyhound Racing NSW to smaller regional track facilities; the role and objectives of the Greyhound Welfare Integrity Commission; greyhound welfare measures, including rehoming programs; and financial decisions of Greyhound Racing NSW, including contract employment arrangements. The objectives of Greyhound Racing NSW need to be expanded to consider the social, cultural and economic factors that are impacted by its decisions. I will therefore seek to amend the governing legislation to ensure that the holistic impacts of decisions by Greyhound Racing NSW need to be a factor in those decisions. I ask every member in Parliament to support continued greyhound racing in regional New South Wales.

Ms KYLIE WILKINSON ( East Hills ) ( 17:46 :38 ): As we approach the end of the year and Christmas, it is the perfect time to recognise the incredible community spirit that defines the East Hills electorate at Christmas time. One of the things I admire most about our community is the way people look out for one another. Whether it is schools, churches, businesses or volunteer groups, there is a genuine commitment to making sure no-one feels alone, especially at this time of year. Across East Hills, our school fetes and end-of-year carnivals bring families together in a way that only school communities can. These events do not just raise funds; they build connection, belonging and pride in our local schools. One example is Padstow Heights Public School's Christmas fair, which I look forward to attending in a couple of weeks.

Our churches play an equally important role. We are fortunate to have many active congregations across our electorate, each running their own internal Christmas donation drives. These groups quietly collect food, gifts and supplies to ensure that families doing it tough feel supported. Organisations like Georges River Life Care continue their year-round support. This year it is again running its "light, hope, joy, strength" Christmas appeal. This provides practical help and emotional support to people who need it most. Another inspiring example of East Hills community spirit is the partnership between Picnic Point High School and Keith's Closet. The Picnic Point High School community came together to deliver more than 30 boxes filled with toiletries and accessories for people accessing mental health services. Every item was thoughtfully wrapped, a simple gesture that will make someone's Christmas a little brighter. The community even dedicated a full day to packing, giving students and families a hands-on opportunity to support others. Keith's Closet's Christmas drives and annual Shoebox Appeal are now in their fifth year. The organisation is aiming for 1,000 boxes and is well on its way. Its work has brought comfort and hope to countless people across Sydney and the East Hills electorate.

Our businesses are also stepping up. The Canterbury Bankstown Chamber of Commerce is running its annual Christmas toy drive, bringing the local business community together to give every child the chance to feel the joy of the season. The efforts of the chamber and local businesses show how strongly our small business owners care for the families they serve. It is such a privilege to be able to deliver these toys to sick kids at our local hospital, bringing a small bit of joy to those facing some of the toughest moments of their young lives. Groups like Anglicare, through initiatives such as Toys 'n' Tucker, continue to support local households with food and presents, making sure Christmas can be a time of celebration, not stress.

We also see this community spirit shine through in our local Christmas carols. Panania Anglican Church is once again hosting their Christmas carols event, bringing together families, neighbours and parish members to celebrate the season in song. Over at Rotary Club of Padstow, they are preparing for their much-loved Carols by Candlelight. This family event continues to draw a huge crowd every year. It has become one of the biggest and most anticipated community gatherings. It lights up the season and gives families a chance to come together in a joyful and meaningful way.

All of these examples show that the East Hills electorate is built on generosity, community and genuine care for others. This spirit is not limited to one organisation or one suburb. It is seen throughout Panania, Revesby, Padstow, East Hills, Condell Park, Georges Hall and every corner of our electorate. I am delighted to formally acknowledge my own Christmas card competition winner, Timothy Zhang, from Panania North Public School. His beautiful Christmas design, including a very Aussie Santa, will be in letterboxes throughout our community very soon.

As we move towards the end of the year, I acknowledge every volunteer, every school, every community organisation or group, every business, every faith organisation, and every family who has contributed to these efforts. They are the reason East Hills remains such a strong, supportive and deeply connected community. To everyone who has given their time, their donations, or simply a moment of kindness, I say thank you for making our electorate a great place to live, and reminding us what community means. I wish everyone a safe and happy holiday season, spent with family and friends, or the person that cares for them most.

tree_branches.text: Dr DAVID SALIBA ( Fairfield ) ( 16:34 :44 ): I recognise the outstanding achievements of the graduates of the leadership program of Shayna Humanitarian Services, in partnership with Unbound Stories and the Institute for Economics and Peace. This year's program focused on building social cohesion and peace by empowering young emerging leaders to take on meaningful roles in their communities. Participants received internationally recognised training, collaborated with local services and developed projects that address antisocial behaviour and support access to education and employment. I commend the 23 graduates of this year's program for their dedication and commitment to making New South Wales better. I extend sincere thanks to all those who supported this initiative, including Oliver Slewa, Multicultural NSW, community leaders and representatives from the NSW Police Force and SBS. Their combined efforts continue to inspire and nurture leadership and harmony across our community.

tree_branches.text: Mr BRENDAN MOYLAN ( Northern Tablelands ) —I recognise Matt Dobbs, local teacher at Glen Innes High School on being honoured with the Prime Minister's Prize for Excellence in Science Teaching in Secondary Schools, in the 2025 Prime Minister's Prizes for Science. Such is the importance of this honour, prizes at these awards are considered Australia's most prestigious and highly regarded Science awards. I congratulate Matt on this outstanding and well-deserved accolade, with his excellence recognised for his many achievements, including: inspiring students with his unwavering commitment to science, technology, engineering and mathematics [STEM] education; going beyond to engage students and mentor teachers in his school and nationwide; promoting STEM to students from a range of backgrounds and teaching students from remote communities of NSW. I commend Matt on his creative teaching methods, extra-curricular activities around science, and for continuing to develop and share his knowledge with others. I thank Matt for his dedication to his students and the school community of Glen Innes High School. Matt's valuable contribution to enriching young people's lives in our community is greatly appreciated.

tree_branches.text: Ms CHARISHMA KALIYANDA ( Liverpool ) ( 16:36 :43 ): I recently had the pleasure of attending the open day hosted by the Australian Islamic Cultural Centre at Masjid Bilal—Bilal Mosque—in Hinchinbrook. This wonderful event created a welcoming space for people of all backgrounds from across the Liverpool community to visit the mosque, meet members of the local Muslim community and deepen their understanding of Islamic culture and traditions. Open days like this are vital in fostering mutual respect and strengthening community bonds. They highlight the important role that mosques play in our local area, not only as places of worship but also as hubs for learning, charity and connection. It was inspiring to see so many residents walk through the doors, engage in meaningful conversations and show genuine interest in the beliefs and practices of their neighbours. These moments of openness and curiosity make our community stronger and more inclusive. I extend my sincere thanks to the Australian Islamic Cultural Centre and the dedicated team at Masjid Bilal for their warm hospitality and for creating such an informative and welcoming day. Their efforts truly help bring our communities closer together.

tree_branches.text: Mrs HELEN DALTON ( Murray ) —Mister Speaker, Today I recognise Deniliquin-based Sergeant Samara Hynes of the NSW Police Force for her outstanding commitment to officer safety and wellbeing. At the 2025 Commissioner's Safety Awards held at Goulburn Police Academy, Sergeant Hynes received both the Commissioner's Perpetual Safety Award and the Voluntary Health and Wellbeing Support Role award for her work supporting colleagues beyond her formal duties. In her role at Deniliquin Police Station, Sergeant Hynes manages seized evidence and property and educates officers in safe handling and packaging—from seizure through to storage—with staff safety and wellbeing front of mind. Beyond her formal duties, she supports young officers who relocate to Deniliquin. She is known for her "mum chats", runs fitness/cross fit sessions at her home to support mental and physical health, checks in on staff in her own time, and recently helped a member of the August 2025 class find accommodation and prepare to settle in before graduation. I congratulate Sergeant Hynes on this well-deserved recognition and thank her for the leadership and compassion she provides to the Deniliquin police and wider community.

tree_branches.text: Ms JULIA FINN ( Granville ) —I acknowledge the important work undertaken at the Community Response to Domestic and Family Violence seminar hosted by Darulfatwa, the Islamic High Council of Australia in Chester Hill on 9 October. Domestic and family violence remains one of the most pressing social challenges across Western Sydney, affecting women, children and families in every cultural, linguistic and faith community. I commend Darulfatwa, under the leadership of Manager Mohamad Chams, for convening this forum and for their ongoing commitment to peace, justice and the wellbeing of local families. By bringing together religious leaders, NSW Police, the Department of Communities and Justice, MetroAssist and Justice Support Centre, the seminar reflected the collective responsibility required to prevent violence and support survivors. The NSW Government is strengthening this work through the Pathways to Prevention: NSW Strategy for the Prevention of Domestic, Family and Sexual Violence 2024–2028 and a $5.2 million investment in community-led prevention programs that promote respectful relationships, healthy masculinities, consent education and gender equality. I thank all involved for their leadership and commitment to building safer, stronger and more respectful communities across Western Sydney.

tree_branches.text: Ms STEPHANIE DI PASQUA ( Drummoyne ) —I rise to acknowledge a local Rhodes resident and author, Dr Uma Srinivasan and to sincerely congratulate her on the launch of her new book 'Etched in Gold'. Etched in Gold is a historical fiction, telling the story of two Indian women connected through their passion for music and their culture throughout the 16th to 18th centuries. The novel is an important reminder of the power of storytelling in sharing histories and preserving cultural heritage. Prior to beginning her journey as an author, Dr Srinivasan worked as a computer scientist, obtaining her PhD from the University of New South Wales. Her transition to literature is a testament to her talent and dedication to lifelong learning. I have known Dr Srinivasan for a number of years during her time serving on the City of Canada Bay Council's Rhodes Community Committee, where she volunteered her time serving Rhodes and working to bring better services for the community. I sincerely congratulate Dr Srinivasan on the release of her novel 'Etched in Gold' and I wish her all the very best.

tree_branches.text: Ms LIESL TESCH ( Gosford ) —Our 2025 Gosford Community Champion Award recipients have blown me away with their kindness, passion and generosity. I would like to acknowledge Lisa Caswell, an incredible woman who has ignited community spirit in many of us while showcasing kindness and bringing smiles to our vulnerable community members. Lisa has dedicated her time at Meals on Wheels Central Coast for several years to help our community members feel safe and independent and well fed. Being the kind spirit Lisa is, she always makes the clients happy when they received their meals from her. From the light-hearted chat to the caring actions, Lisa has provided more than just food because to some of these community members, seeing Lisa might be the best thing happened in their week. Meals on Wheels is an important organisation on the Central Coast and with people like Lisa, who have been modelling true community champion that make Meals on Wheels extra special to our community. I thank the fabulous Lisa Caswell for her compassion and kindness towards the Meals on Wheels community.

tree_branches.text: Mr DAVID LAYZELL ( Upper Hunter ) —I want to acknowledge the ongoing work in the Upper Hunter to improve road safety starting with our newest road users. Upper Hunter Shire Council and Hunter Valley Police District began the Learner Night Driver Program in late-2024 and it is being strongly supported by the community. Hunter Learner Night Drive is for learner drivers of any age, who must be accompanied by an appropriately licenced supervisor aged over 25. The event exposes learner drivers to real life driving scenarios and the opportunity to interact with police in a controlled environment. Learner drivers use a track at Scone Airport and get to experience stationary and mobile breath tests with police as well as receiving advice and guidance on how to safely undertake these tasks. The track includes a section where drivers can practice reverse parallel parking, roadcraft and vehicle manoeuvring. Learner Night Drive is supported by Hunter Valley Highway Patrol, Transport for NSW, NSW Ambulance, Singleton Council, Muswellbrook Shire Council and Merriwa VRA. I also want to acknowledge the corporate supporters assisting this initiative including JBS Scone, Bengalla Mining Company, Pays Air Service and Hunter Warbirds.

tree_branches.text: Mr JASON LI ( Strathfield ) —I rise to recognise the tremendous success of this year's Burwood Greek Street Fair, a much-loved celebration that continues to highlight Burwood as one of Sydney's most culturally diverse and welcoming communities. The Fair brings the vibrant spirit and timeless tradition of the outdoor Greek panigiri, a centuries-old festival, to the heart of Sydney and it has rightly become one of Burwood's most anticipated cultural events. The event showcased wonderful music, dance, food and family-friendly entertainment that reflected both Greek heritage and our shared community pride. I acknowledge and thank Burwood Council for its continued partnership and support and extend special recognition to The Greek Orthodox Parish and Community of Burwood and District, Saint Nectarios, whose dedication and volunteering make this celebration possible each year. It was a pleasure to attend and to witness the strong community engagement, with so many local families, businesses, schools and cultural groups joining together in such a joyful atmosphere. My warm congratulations and thanks go to everyone involved, and I look forward to celebrating again next year.
