tree_branches.text: Ms KATELIN McINERNEY ( Ki ama ) —I would like to recognise Mark Burns, the founder of The Man Walk, for his outstanding contribution to men's health and wellbeing in our community and across Australia. Beginning in Kiama in 2019, Mark launched a simple idea with powerful intent: to create a space where men could walk, talk, and support one another without judgement. Since then, The Man Walk has grown to over 80 locations nationwide, with more than 130,000 men taking part. Through Mark's leadership, thousands of men have found connection, routine, mateship, and a safe place to speak openly about the challenges they face. Countless participants credit The Man Walk with improving their mental health, building lasting friendships, and, in some cases, changing or even saving lives. Mark's vision has sparked a movement rooted in compassion and community strength. We thank him for walking alongside so many and for inspiring a culture of reaching out for support.

Mr ROBERT DWYER ( Port Macquarie ) —I want to pay tribute to the remarkable volunteers of the Moorland Rural Fire Brigade, whose tireless efforts to protect our community reflect the highest standards of service and dedication. These individuals respond to bushfires, motor vehicle incidents, and severe weather emergencies, often working under dangerous conditions to safeguard lives and property across the Port Macquarie-Hastings and Mid Coast regions. Their contribution is not only brave—it is vital. The brigade plays a key role in strengthening local resilience, particularly during bushfire season. Beyond emergency response, they actively engage in community education and preparedness initiatives, helping residents stay informed and ready. They are often called away from the local area to support fire activities in other areas. The impact of their work reaches far beyond immediate safety. By reducing disaster risks and supporting recovery, they help protect local businesses, tourism, and infrastructure, while fostering unity and pride within our community. I commend Captain Stewart Waugh, Senior Deputy Captain Michael Hudson and every member of the Moorland Rural Fire Brigade for their unwavering commitment, bravery, and service. Their work strengthens our communities and ensures we are safer, better prepared, and more united in the face of adversity.

Mr ALISTER HENSKENS ( Wahroonga ) ( 16:51 :40 ): I acknowledge the outstanding contributions of community organisations in my electorate of Wahroonga, with some receiving funding under the Community Building Partnership program. I wholeheartedly support initiatives that strengthen our communities and deliver real benefits to local people. This year's grants have funded a diverse range of projects that improve safety, enhance education, promote health and wellbeing, and foster inclusion in the Wahroonga electorate. They are tangible improvements that will make a difference in the daily lives of thousands of residents in my community, and I am pleased to be able to support them in that way.

At PCYC Hornsby-Ku-ring-gai, a grant of $18,000 will provide new gym equipment, including a pendulum squat machine and SkiErg. The upgrade benefits gym members, local sporting teams, school sport programs and police initiatives, and helps young people build strength and confidence while engaging in activities that promote wellbeing, whether at the Mark Taylor Oval in Waitara or elsewhere. Education is a cornerstone of our community, and several schools have received vital support in this round of grants. The Wahroonga Public School's P&C Association received $100,000 to resurface sports courts and cricket nets. That will create multi‑sport spaces for students and the wider community after the public school had not received a Community Building Partnership grant for some years. The Normanhurst Public School's P&C Association received $25,000 to continue its sensory garden project, which will transform unused space into an inclusive outdoor learning environment.

The Pymble Public School's P&C Association received $30,000 to upgrade play equipment for students in years 3 to 6, which will create a safe and engaging space for over 300 students every day. The Pennant Hills High School's P&C Association received $38,657 for shaded seating areas, which will give students comfortable spaces to learn and socialise outdoors. That is incredibly important to the school's outdoor learning areas. The Normanhurst Boys High School's P&C Association received $10,000 to upgrade its canteen furniture, which will improve wellbeing and interaction for students and volunteers.

Sporting organisations are also benefiting from this round of grants. The Kissing Point Sports Club received $7,014 to upgrade coaching equipment and introduce a uniform hire program to encourage participation in netball. It also received $15,000 for audiovisual equipment to enhance the clubhouse experience for members and volunteers. The Kissing Point Sports Club is one of the largest sporting clubs in my electorate. Meanwhile, Thornleigh Sports Club—another big multi-sports club in the electorate—received $12,540 to restore the cricket pitch and surrounding areas at Thornleigh Oval, which will ensure safe and playable grounds for local competitions. That has been an issue for some years because of bad weather.

Community safety and wellbeing remain priorities for the allocation of funding. The 2nd Turramurra Scout Group received $27,817 to replace deteriorated hall eaves and fascia boards, remove hazardous asbestos and install a defibrillator. They are critical improvements that will protect health and extend the life of that important facility, which is completely maintained by volunteers and grants of this kind. Streetwork Australia Limited received $12,735 to upgrade iPads for youth caseworkers to enable better delivery of programs that support vulnerable young people. Lifeline Harbour to Hawkesbury Sydney received $33,916 to replace its van, which will ensure the continued collection and delivery of pre-loved goods that fund life-saving mental health services.

Faith and cultural organisations have not been forgotten. The Danish Church in Australia received $10,000 to create a covered outdoor area, which will offer a safe and welcoming space for children and community members to gather. Similarly, Thornleigh Community Baptist Church received $61,456 to refurbish its auditorium and adjoining office, which will improve facilities that serve a wide range of community groups. Some of our youngest learners will benefit from this round of grants too. Uniting Preschool Turramurra - TurraTots received $20,000 to resurface its verandah play area, which will enhance safety and comfort for children during active play and learning.

Finally, we are supporting emerging sports. The Sydney Northern Rays Water Polo Club received $27,865 to acquire a timing board and scoreboard. That will help the growing club provide better experiences for players and spectators. Those projects demonstrate the importance of governments investing in local communities. Unfortunately, the Minns Labor Government has not made any significant investments in my local community.

tree_branches.name: Ms KYLIE WILKINSON
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > East Hills Electorate Sports Photo Competition > Ms KYLIE WILKINSON
tree_branches.text:
Ms KYLIE WILKINSON ( East Hills ) ( 17:46 :38 ): As we approach the end of the year and Christmas, it is the perfect time to recognise the incredible community spirit that defines the East Hills electorate at Christmas time. One of the things I admire most about our community is the way people look out for one another. Whether it is schools, churches, businesses or volunteer groups, there is a genuine commitment to making sure no-one feels alone, especially at this time of year. Across East Hills, our school fetes and end-of-year carnivals bring families together in a way that only school communities can. These events do not just raise funds; they build connection, belonging and pride in our local schools. One example is Padstow Heights Public School's Christmas fair, which I look forward to attending in a couple of weeks.

Our churches play an equally important role. We are fortunate to have many active congregations across our electorate, each running their own internal Christmas donation drives. These groups quietly collect food, gifts and supplies to ensure that families doing it tough feel supported. Organisations like Georges River Life Care continue their year-round support. This year it is again running its "light, hope, joy, strength" Christmas appeal. This provides practical help and emotional support to people who need it most. Another inspiring example of East Hills community spirit is the partnership between Picnic Point High School and Keith's Closet. The Picnic Point High School community came together to deliver more than 30 boxes filled with toiletries and accessories for people accessing mental health services. Every item was thoughtfully wrapped, a simple gesture that will make someone's Christmas a little brighter. The community even dedicated a full day to packing, giving students and families a hands-on opportunity to support others. Keith's Closet's Christmas drives and annual Shoebox Appeal are now in their fifth year. The organisation is aiming for 1,000 boxes and is well on its way. Its work has brought comfort and hope to countless people across Sydney and the East Hills electorate.

Our businesses are also stepping up. The Canterbury Bankstown Chamber of Commerce is running its annual Christmas toy drive, bringing the local business community together to give every child the chance to feel the joy of the season. The efforts of the chamber and local businesses show how strongly our small business owners care for the families they serve. It is such a privilege to be able to deliver these toys to sick kids at our local hospital, bringing a small bit of joy to those facing some of the toughest moments of their young lives. Groups like Anglicare, through initiatives such as Toys 'n' Tucker, continue to support local households with food and presents, making sure Christmas can be a time of celebration, not stress.

We also see this community spirit shine through in our local Christmas carols. Panania Anglican Church is once again hosting their Christmas carols event, bringing together families, neighbours and parish members to celebrate the season in song. Over at Rotary Club of Padstow, they are preparing for their much-loved Carols by Candlelight. This family event continues to draw a huge crowd every year. It has become one of the biggest and most anticipated community gatherings. It lights up the season and gives families a chance to come together in a joyful and meaningful way.

All of these examples show that the East Hills electorate is built on generosity, community and genuine care for others. This spirit is not limited to one organisation or one suburb. It is seen throughout Panania, Revesby, Padstow, East Hills, Condell Park, Georges Hall and every corner of our electorate. I am delighted to formally acknowledge my own Christmas card competition winner, Timothy Zhang, from Panania North Public School. His beautiful Christmas design, including a very Aussie Santa, will be in letterboxes throughout our community very soon.

As we move towards the end of the year, I acknowledge every volunteer, every school, every community organisation or group, every business, every faith organisation, and every family who has contributed to these efforts. They are the reason East Hills remains such a strong, supportive and deeply connected community. To everyone who has given their time, their donations, or simply a moment of kindness, I say thank you for making our electorate a great place to live, and reminding us what community means. I wish everyone a safe and happy holiday season, spent with family and friends, or the person that cares for them most.

Mr MICHAEL REGAN ( Wakehurst ) ( 17:41 :35 ): Brookvale Public School is the fifth smallest school on the northern beaches, with around 310 students enrolled in 2025. However, it may be small in numbers but it is bursting with spirit. The tight‑knit school is a place of social connection, belonging and purpose. The dedicated staff nurture every child, supporting them to flourish. The school has a rich program of extracurricular activities and also supports academic excellence, hosting an opportunity class since the beginning of this year. The thriving school culture is testament to the commitment of all the teachers, mums and dad, and the great kids at the school. Tonight I acknowledge and thank the entire school community, particularly principal Mr Luke Richmond for his excellent leadership. Brookvale is one of many excellent public schools in my electorate of Wakehurst, but right now it is facing some unique pressures.

For over a year, the Brookvale P&C has raised legitimate concerns about high school catchment boundaries. Currently, Brookvale Public School falls in the catchment area for the Northern Beaches Secondary College Cromer Campus without access to local single sex school options. The department has said that will continue, even though the nearby Northern Beaches Secondary College Freshwater Senior Campus is transitioning to a comprehensive years 7 to 12 high school from 2027 and the new Forest High School is opening in Allambie Height, the suburb right next door. The clear request from the Brookvale P&C is to include Brookvale in the intake area for the new years 7 to 12 Freshwater campus. I am also keen to see maximum choice for Brookvale families, including opening up Forest High School, Mackellar Girls Campus and Balgowlah Boys' Campus.

There are several reasons why keeping Brookvale zoned to Cromer campus is illogical and including it in the Freshwater catchment makes a lot more sense. Firstly, is geographic accessibility: Freshwater campus will be the closest high school, just 1.4 kilometres away from Brookvale Public School. It is mostly flat and a walkable or rideable distance from home for many Brookvale students. Cromer campus is much further away, involving a longer and more complex commute of up to 45 minutes, including multiple bus transfers. Over six years of high school that is about 1,800 hours commuting, equivalent to almost a full school year spent just travelling.

Secondly, is about maintaining community connectedness. Listening to the parent body at Brookvale, the reality is their networks of sports and social activities are the same as the families who will attend the Freshwater campus. Brookvale children train and play with Brookvale Football Club in Manly, play netball at Curl Curl, or are members of Surf Life Saving clubs at Freshwater and Curl Curl, among countless other engagements. We need to encourage continuity and depth of social connection, for both parents and students, across different parts of their lives. Thirdly, and very importantly, there is a fairness, equity and inclusion dimension to this issue. The position statement from Brookvale P&C states:

The decision to exclude Brookvale from the Freshwater Campus intake also appears to deepen class-based inequalities in the Northern Beaches public school system. Brookvale is home to a far more diverse mix of ethnic, cultural, and socio-economic backgrounds than many surrounding suburbs. Yet, we are being cut off from the high school options being made available to wealthier areas like Freshwater, Curl Curl, Manly and Balgowlah.

Brookvale students and families should get the same choices and opportunities as surrounding suburbs. Brookvale is a small school, so we are talking about a low number of students each year, which will have minimal impact on numbers at the Freshwater campus. The Brookvale Public School community feels that, in both process and outcome, the current high school zoning decision is unjustified and unfair. Frankly, I agree with them. I will not go into the details, but I think the Department of Education could have been more responsive and transparent on this issue.

I thank the members of the P&C, particularly president Hina Osmany, for being so engaged, eloquent and persistent in their advocacy. Brookvale is a small school doing great things. It needs to be celebrated, maintained and supported, not undermined. I have made clear to the education Minister's office my strong view that Brookvale primary students should be zoned for Freshwater campus from day one in 2027. Depending on capacity, I also think Brookvale students should have the option of Forest High, Mackellar Girls or Balgowlah Boys. I have also sought and received the following commitments from the education Minister's office: firstly, for the education Minister to meet with the P&C leadership before the beginning of the 2026 school year; secondly, for an expression of interest survey process for students in years 4, 5 and 6 at Brookvale to get an accurate picture of their high school preferences and the numbers of students; and, thirdly, at the very least for there to be a catchment review in 2027, taking into account actual enrolments across all schools impacted by the zoning changes. However, I am pushing for this to happen in late 2026 so that, if possible, students can start at their preferred high school in 2027.

I have also requested that if Brookvale students are not included in the Freshwater campus catchment from day one in 2027, they should have formal out‑of‑area enrolment priority at Freshwater, Forest High, Mackellar Girls and Balgowlah Boys. I will continue to push for this and keep the community updated. School catchment boundaries may be lines on a map for the Department of Education, but for students and families these are life‑changing delineations. Decisions about school catchments need to be made with local insight and proper consultation. The wrong call has been made in this case, and I will keep pushing for a fairer, commonsense outcome for Brookvale families.

tree_branches.name: Wahroonga Electorate Community Building Partnership Grants

tree_branches.text:
At PCYC Hornsby-Ku-ring-gai, a grant of $18,000 will provide new gym equipment, including a pendulum squat machine and SkiErg. The upgrade benefits gym members, local sporting teams, school sport programs and police initiatives, and helps young people build strength and confidence while engaging in activities that promote wellbeing, whether at the Mark Taylor Oval in Waitara or elsewhere. Education is a cornerstone of our community, and several schools have received vital support in this round of grants. The Wahroonga Public School's P&C Association received $100,000 to resurface sports courts and cricket nets. That will create multi‑sport spaces for students and the wider community after the public school had not received a Community Building Partnership grant for some years. The Normanhurst Public School's P&C Association received $25,000 to continue its sensory garden project, which will transform unused space into an inclusive outdoor learning environment.

The Pymble Public School's P&C Association received $30,000 to upgrade play equipment for students in years 3 to 6, which will create a safe and engaging space for over 300 students every day. The Pennant Hills High School's P&C Association received $38,657 for shaded seating areas, which will give students comfortable spaces to learn and socialise outdoors. That is incredibly important to the school's outdoor learning areas. The Normanhurst Boys High School's P&C Association received $10,000 to upgrade its canteen furniture, which will improve wellbeing and interaction for students and volunteers.

Sporting organisations are also benefiting from this round of grants. The Kissing Point Sports Club received $7,014 to upgrade coaching equipment and introduce a uniform hire program to encourage participation in netball. It also received $15,000 for audiovisual equipment to enhance the clubhouse experience for members and volunteers. The Kissing Point Sports Club is one of the largest sporting clubs in my electorate. Meanwhile, Thornleigh Sports Club—another big multi-sports club in the electorate—received $12,540 to restore the cricket pitch and surrounding areas at Thornleigh Oval, which will ensure safe and playable grounds for local competitions. That has been an issue for some years because of bad weather.

Community safety and wellbeing remain priorities for the allocation of funding. The 2nd Turramurra Scout Group received $27,817 to replace deteriorated hall eaves and fascia boards, remove hazardous asbestos and install a defibrillator. They are critical improvements that will protect health and extend the life of that important facility, which is completely maintained by volunteers and grants of this kind. Streetwork Australia Limited received $12,735 to upgrade iPads for youth caseworkers to enable better delivery of programs that support vulnerable young people. Lifeline Harbour to Hawkesbury Sydney received $33,916 to replace its van, which will ensure the continued collection and delivery of pre-loved goods that fund life-saving mental health services.

Faith and cultural organisations have not been forgotten. The Danish Church in Australia received $10,000 to create a covered outdoor area, which will offer a safe and welcoming space for children and community members to gather. Similarly, Thornleigh Community Baptist Church received $61,456 to refurbish its auditorium and adjoining office, which will improve facilities that serve a wide range of community groups. Some of our youngest learners will benefit from this round of grants too. Uniting Preschool Turramurra - TurraTots received $20,000 to resurface its verandah play area, which will enhance safety and comfort for children during active play and learning.

That will help the growing club provide better experiences for players and spectators. Those projects demonstrate the importance of governments investing in local communities. Unfortunately, the Minns Labor Government has not made any significant investments in my local community.

tree_branches.name: Grace Kennedy
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Grace Kennedy
tree_branches.text:
The International Surfing Association has worked closely with the International Paralympic Committee to refine classification systems and ensure that athletes are recognised for their skill, courage and performance, and not defined by their disability. Through those efforts, para surfing has built a clear pathway for athletes to train, compete and represent their nations at the highest level. The sport builds resilience, confidence and community values that mirror the very best of the Paralympic movement. At its heart, disabled surfing plays a vital role in fostering social inclusion. Across the South Coast—and, indeed, across Australia—we see volunteers, coaches and clubs opening the doors of our beaches to everyone. Organisations such as the Disabled Surfers Association and community-led initiatives make it possible for people of all ages and abilities to experience the freedom of the ocean.

The beach has long been part of our Australian identity. It is a place where barriers fall away, where laughter is shared and where community thrives. Through surfing, we see friendships formed, confidence restored and people rediscovering their sense of purpose. It is inclusion in its purest form, and it is achieved not through policy or theory but through compassion, connection and courage. With the assistance of people such as Grace and James Gissing from Good Surf, I want to see para surfing become part of everyday boardriding clubs throughout New South Wales. I am putting Ulladulla Boardriders on notice. I am coming their way very soon to begin this important initiative. Including para surfing in the Paralympic Games would be a natural and powerful next step. The sport already meets the standards of international competition, classification and governance. More importantly, it embodies the Paralympic values of determination, equality and inspiration.

Grace Kennedy's success is living proof that our para surfers are ready. Grace's bronze medal on the world stage shows not only her exceptional talent but also the strength of Australian coaches like James Gissing, our volunteers and our community spirit that supports athletes from the shoreline to the world arena. By welcoming para surfing into the Paralympics, we would give recognition to thousands of athletes who have trained tirelessly, often without funding or fanfare, to demonstrate what true resilience looks like. We would affirm, on a global stage, that sport belongs to everyone.

Grace Kennedy's journey reminds us that the ocean belongs to all of us; it does not see ability or disability, only determination and spirit. Grace's achievement inspires every young person watching from our South Coast beaches and every person with a disability who dreams of feeling the spray of the ocean on their face. It is time that para surfing, a sport that so perfectly captures Australia's love of the ocean and our belief in inclusion, is recognised on the world's greatest stage, the Paralympic Games. I congratulate Grace, and every para surfer blazing a trail for equality and recognition. They have not only made their community proud, but they have made a powerful case for a more inclusive future in sport, and in life.

tree_branches.name: Ms LIZA BUTLER
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Grace Kennedy > Ms LIZA BUTLER
tree_branches.text: Ms LIZA BUTLER ( South Coast ) —I am delighted to recognise and celebrate the inspiring young artists whose work is now shining at the Shoalhaven Regional Gallery in Nowra. The latest exhibition showcases artwork created through the HOME Program, a powerful initiative inviting students from Falls Creek, Greenwell Point, Nowra, Sanctuary Point and Tomerong Public Schools to explore the meaning of 'home'. Over three school terms, these students connected deeply with local Aboriginal artists, community, language and culture. Guided by the talents of Aunty Cheryl Davison, Aunty Deidre Martin and cultural knowledge holder Allen Bloxsome, the students took part in workshops and virtual excursions that enriched their understanding and sparked their creativity. The HOME Program offers young people a meaningful opportunity to engage with First Nations stories, culture and history, building respect, understanding and a stronger connection to the land they call home. The artworks on display reflect this journey with honesty, depth and skill. I extend my heartfelt congratulations to every student artist, to the educators who supported them, and to the First Nations artists and partners who made this program possible. Their collective effort has created an exhibition our community can be proud of.

tree_branches.name: Renewable Energy
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Renewable Energy
tree_branches.text:
The entire plan is based on hope that transmission will magically appear on time, hope that the batteries will be built someday, and hope that the wind will always blow and the sun will always shine. Hope is not an energy policy. Meanwhile, regional New South Wales is being carved up like it does not matter. Prime farmland is being bulldozed for solar factories. Wind turbines taller than skyscrapers—as tall as 300 metres in some cases—are being dumped next to family homes. Transmission lines are cutting straight through communities, without proper consultation or compensation. Locals are being inconvenienced. They are being promised jobs and benefits, but there is very little of that in many communities.

The rollout is a farce because it is being driven by ideology. People are drawing on whiteboards and turning up in hard hats for photo opportunities, but the Government is far more interested in looking green than actually delivering power that works. The truth is simple: We need to make sure that we have proper energy supply in the State, but that should not be at the expense of regional communities. We certainly cannot expect regional communities to take all the pain just so the Government can tick a box. The Government needs to get real, with proper planning, proven technology and proper community consultation. New South Wales is being marched towards an energy disaster of the Government's own making. That current pathway is reckless and chaotic. The people of New South Wales deserve better.

The reckless renewable rollout is not only affecting the regions. We hear from those in the city that regional areas who do not want it are nimbys. Regional communities are bearing the brunt of the entire renewable rollout. It is no wonder metro MPs do not care. Before the last election, only 18 carefully considered renewable energy projects were approved. In the past 2½ years alone, over 60 have been approved and many more are racing to get into the pipeline. Each project proposed is getting the rubber stamp of approval before the ink dries on the proposal. The Government's agenda is clear. This week the public interest debate was about renewable energy. We heard comments from the Premier that they are not going to slow it down. They are going to continue to fast‑track renewable projects in regional communities.

Regional communities are being disadvantaged by the rollout of the projects. The Government needs to make sure that our communities are heard. Members in this place are making decisions on behalf of communities that they have not even met with or listened to. Ministers have not even bothered to front up to community meetings, or spoken to those people who will be impacted to see how their lives will be turned upside down. Local councils are moving motions at local government conferences. Renewable energy projects are being forced on our communities, and people are sick and tired of it. Our farmers have been working the land, our small towns have been held together, and our communities want to continue to work in those areas. The people feel that the impact of the projects do not allow them and their voices to be heard.

tree_branches.name: Westmead Institute for Medical Research
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Westmead Institute for Medical Research
tree_branches.text:
For over two decades, WIMR has been at the forefront of scientific discovery, driving clinical innovation and delivering translational research that changes lives. Its researchers are tackling some of the most urgent health challenges of our time, from cancer, infectious diseases and neurological disorders to diabetes, liver disease and cardiovascular conditions. What sets WIMR apart is not only the scale and quality of its research but its unwavering commitment to improving human health both in Australia and globally. Its work is recognised internationally and is a source of immense pride for our local community in Parramatta.

I recently had the opportunity to visit Phage Australia, based at WIMR, and was truly inspired by the remarkable work taking place inside those laboratories. Phage Australia is leading the charge in phage therapy, an exciting and rapidly developing area of medicine that offers a targeted alternative to antibiotics. That is especially important in the face of growing antimicrobial resistance, which is one of the most serious public health threats of our time.

A significant milestone has been the establishment of Australia's first phage biomanufacturing facility, backed by the New South Wales Government. The state-of-the-art facility enables the clinical translation and scalable production of phage-based therapies—a critical step forward for Australian medical research and treatment capabilities. During my visit, I met with Professor Jon Iredell, Director of Phage Australia, and heard compelling stories of patients whose lives have been transformed by the therapy. One young person, facing the terrifying prospect of amputation, made a full recovery thanks to phage treatment. These are not just medical breakthroughs; they are stories of hope, resilience and lives being changed for the better.

The phage biomanufacturing facility has provided access to life- and limb-saving phage therapy for patients around Australia through a $3.5 million New South Wales Government investment in 2023. I thank Minister Harris for his ongoing support for all that Phage Australia is doing in this groundbreaking field of medicine. I know that, on the day he made the current funding announcement, he met with Professor Iredell, along with researchers from the United States, the United Kingdom and South Korea who were visiting to learn from that world‑leading research program.

The program is also a powerful reminder of the life-saving innovation happening in Western Sydney. Often we walk past those buildings without knowing the incredible work underway inside—research and development that has the potential to change the future of medicine not only in New South Wales and Australia but also around the world. Australia is globally respected for the quality of our medical research, and institutions like WIMR are a shining example of that strength. They do not just advance science; they build partnerships, train future leaders and address health inequities in our communities.

One of the most impressive aspects of my visit to Phage was the women working in that place. It was inspiring to see the role that they were playing in that incredibly important world-leading research and to hear the stories of where they started and where they have come to. I thank everyone at the Westmead Institute for Medical Research, especially Executive Director Professor Phillip O'Connell. Their work saves lives, brings hope and showcases the very best of Australian research, innovation, science and compassion, and our potential to lead the world in manufacturing. I commend the achievements of WIMR and reaffirm my strong support for its continued success and future impact.

tree_branches.name: Ms DONNA DAVIS
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Westmead Institute for Medical Research > Ms DONNA DAVIS
tree_branches.text: Ms DONNA DAVIS ( Parramatta ) —I was delighted to join the community on Saturday 1st November for Foundation Day, celebrating Parramatta's proud history and heritage. This year Foundation Day was held at Hambledon Cottage, providing an opportunity to introduce this State heritage listed site to a wider audience as families, friends and even a few four-legged locals enjoyed the free family event. Foundation Day marks the arrival of Governor Arthur Phillip in Parramatta on 2 November 1788 and the start of agricultural projects in the area. The date has traditionally been celebrated with large civic events, street carnivals and parades. In more recent years the actual day has become less of a focus than the sharing of Parramatta's heritage and stories. This year visitors enjoyed guided tours of Hambledon Cottage, horse drawn carriage rides, weaving and blacksmith demonstrations, roving entertainment, children's workshops, face painting an animal farm and entertainment from the Parramatta's City Band. Congratulations to the Parramatta and Districts Historical Society, the City of Parramatta, the Parramatta Lions Club and all who were involved in making the day a success.

tree_branches.name: Artificial Intelligence
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Artificial Intelligence
tree_branches.text:
One of the key concerns raised during the workshop was the increasing use of AI in cybersecurity and defence. AI is not only being used by democratic governments; it is also being used by malicious actors to automate cyber attacks, spread ransomware and exploit vulnerabilities at a scale we have never seen before. Bad actors, whether they are state‑based or criminal organisations, are using AI to conduct sophisticated phishing attacks, generate malicious code and disrupt critical infrastructure. The rapid pace of technological development means that, if we as legislators are not proactive, we will fall behind those who seek to do harm.

AI is being used to generate disinformation to distort the political process through fear and reputational harm using deepfakes and synthetic media. Women, minority groups and community leaders are often targeted and public trust is being undermined. Existing State and national laws are not keeping pace with emerging threats and there are few useful laws elsewhere that we can adopt. We need to modernise laws to prevent the misuse of AI, including preventing harmful AI‑generated content, strengthening regulatory bodies and ensuring tech companies are held accountable for the spread of misinformation on their platforms. But regulation alone will not safeguard democracy. We must invest in digital literacy so that people have the tools and knowledge to navigate the emerging digital environment safely. Firewalls and encryption are not enough; people need to understand the threats and uses of AI.

Artificial intelligence can further entrench digital colonialism. Digital colonialism is the concept where technology helps to subjugate already vulnerable communities through the extraction of data without fair return, through environmental impacts on low-income communities and through the concentration of power and decisions in the wealthy few. Australia and New South Wales have a role to play in challenging that imbalance by promoting fairness, transparency and respect for digital sovereignty and by monitoring the impacts of technological progress on human rights, equity and the environment. We can partner with like‑minded democratic nations to work through the challenges together.

Collaboration will be essential as AI governance cannot be approached in isolation. Technology crosses boundaries, with most cybersecurity threats coming from overseas agents. We should continue to engage actively in international forums, sharing best practices, supporting regional partners and advocating for strong, enforceable standards that balance innovation with accountability. Artificial intelligence provides significant opportunities to advance our economy, health care and governance, and to help us find solutions to challenges like climate change. But we have a responsibility at all levels of government to ensure that it is not used for harm. I call on the Government to work towards laws that promote safe AI use that does not undermine democracy and safety and that prioritises people over profits and big tech.

tree_branches.name: Assyrian Australian Community
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Assyrian Australian Community
tree_branches.text:
As the State member for Prospect, I have been fortunate to meet many remarkable multicultural organisations across our diverse Western Sydney community. Each of them plays an integral role, caring for individuals and maintaining and promoting culture. As their representative in Parliament, I have been proud to stand before this House to share their rich culture and help advocate for their communities. The Sydney chapter of the Assyrian Democratic Movement [ADM]—or Zowaa—is a leading example. Based in the Prospect electorate, the ADM is an active social and political organisation whose members strive to preserve and protect Assyrian culture. Their advocacy efforts strengthen our Assyrian‑Australian community in Western Sydney and in their traditional homelands, including the Nineveh Plains and the city of Mosul.

Recently I was pleased to meet with a delegation from the ADM's political bureau in Iraq, Ninab Yousif Toma and Ashur Slewa Nico. I thank Immanuel Sada and George Adam from the ADM Sydney chapter for introducing me to those great individuals. During our discussion, I was moved to hear of the ADM's fight for the democratic rights of its communities. For over four decades, its members have fought, through prison, persecution and martyrdom, for an Iraq that honours all its peoples without distinction. To this day, they are still fighting and advocating for national partnership. The ADM's story is etched with tragedy: the massacre at Simele in 1933, the destruction of Sorya in 1969, the terrors of the Ba'athist years and the darkness of ISIS. Yet through every storm, its members have persisted. Each epoch tested their endurance, but their advocacy remained steadfast and peaceful, born from spiritual strength and an abiding love for their homeland.

Today the ADM—in Western Sydney and at their bureau in Iraq—calls for partnership. The movement calls upon Iraq to fulfil the promise of its own constitution: to uphold Article 125 of the constitution, guaranteeing cultural, linguistic, and political rights; to amend laws that allow the forced Islamisation of minors; to reform the quota system that silences smaller voices; and to acknowledge, at last, the Chaldean‑Syriac‑Assyrian people as the original inhabitants of Iraq. The ADM requests that on 1 April the Babylonian and Assyrian New Year be designated a national holiday. Above all, the people seek to live alongside their compatriots in peace, with their minority rights respected and contributing, as they always have, to the progress and unity of Iraq. In a century that has too often forgotten the lessons of coexistence, the ADM's vision of partnership is a balm to the politics of division. It sends a clear message that diversity is not a threat; it is, in fact, a foundation.

The Assyrian Australian diaspora is strengthening the social, cultural and economic fabric of New South Wales. In suburbs like Smithfield, Fairfield, Wetherill Park, Prairiewood, Wakeley, Edensor Park and Bossley Park, our Assyrian community has built its roots, with churches like St Mary's Assyrian Church of the East and St Thomas The Apostle Chaldean Diocese to schools like St Narsai Assyrian Christian College and St Hurmizd Primary School. Our Assyrian Australian community are preserving their language, culture and faith whilst embracing the values, traditions and democratic freedoms of Australia. They are living proof that diversity, when respected, is a foundation for strength. This attests to their call for representation and parity in Iraq, calls which are echoed across the Prospect electorate. I am proud to stand in support of our Assyrian Australian community in the hope that one day their people will live freely and securely as respected owners of and equals in their ancestral homelands.

tree_branches.name: Dr HUGH McDERMOTT
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Assyrian Australian Community > Dr HUGH McDERMOTT
tree_branches.text:
Dr HUGH McDERMOTT ( Prospect ) ( 17:16 :06 ): I give my voice to a people whose history runs deeper than the rivers of Mesopotamia: the Chaldean‑Syriac‑Assyrian people of Iraq. For millennia they have carried the torch of civilisation. They are the inheritors of Babylon and Nineveh; guardians of law, literature and faith; and the keepers of one of the world's oldest languages—a dialect spoken by Christ. Yet in the modern era they have endured dispossession, displacement and denial—not for want of love for their homeland but because of the failure of others to recognise that the soil of Iraq belongs to all its children.

As the State member for Prospect, I have been fortunate to meet many remarkable multicultural organisations across our diverse Western Sydney community. Each of them plays an integral role, caring for individuals and maintaining and promoting culture. As their representative in Parliament, I have been proud to stand before this House to share their rich culture and help advocate for their communities. The Sydney chapter of the Assyrian Democratic Movement [ADM]—or Zowaa—is a leading example. Based in the Prospect electorate, the ADM is an active social and political organisation whose members strive to preserve and protect Assyrian culture. Their advocacy efforts strengthen our Assyrian‑Australian community in Western Sydney and in their traditional homelands, including the Nineveh Plains and the city of Mosul.

Recently I was pleased to meet with a delegation from the ADM's political bureau in Iraq, Ninab Yousif Toma and Ashur Slewa Nico. I thank Immanuel Sada and George Adam from the ADM Sydney chapter for introducing me to those great individuals. During our discussion, I was moved to hear of the ADM's fight for the democratic rights of its communities. For over four decades, its members have fought, through prison, persecution and martyrdom, for an Iraq that honours all its peoples without distinction. To this day, they are still fighting and advocating for national partnership. The ADM's story is etched with tragedy: the massacre at Simele in 1933, the destruction of Sorya in 1969, the terrors of the Ba'athist years and the darkness of ISIS. Yet through every storm, its members have persisted. Each epoch tested their endurance, but their advocacy remained steadfast and peaceful, born from spiritual strength and an abiding love for their homeland.

Today the ADM—in Western Sydney and at their bureau in Iraq—calls for partnership. The movement calls upon Iraq to fulfil the promise of its own constitution: to uphold Article 125 of the constitution, guaranteeing cultural, linguistic, and political rights; to amend laws that allow the forced Islamisation of minors; to reform the quota system that silences smaller voices; and to acknowledge, at last, the Chaldean‑Syriac‑Assyrian people as the original inhabitants of Iraq. The ADM requests that on 1 April the Babylonian and Assyrian New Year be designated a national holiday. Above all, the people seek to live alongside their compatriots in peace, with their minority rights respected and contributing, as they always have, to the progress and unity of Iraq. In a century that has too often forgotten the lessons of coexistence, the ADM's vision of partnership is a balm to the politics of division. It sends a clear message that diversity is not a threat; it is, in fact, a foundation.

The Assyrian Australian diaspora is strengthening the social, cultural and economic fabric of New South Wales. In suburbs like Smithfield, Fairfield, Wetherill Park, Prairiewood, Wakeley, Edensor Park and Bossley Park, our Assyrian community has built its roots, with churches like St Mary's Assyrian Church of the East and St Thomas The Apostle Chaldean Diocese to schools like St Narsai Assyrian Christian College and St Hurmizd Primary School. Our Assyrian Australian community are preserving their language, culture and faith whilst embracing the values, traditions and democratic freedoms of Australia. They are living proof that diversity, when respected, is a foundation for strength. This attests to their call for representation and parity in Iraq, calls which are echoed across the Prospect electorate. I am proud to stand in support of our Assyrian Australian community in the hope that one day their people will live freely and securely as respected owners of and equals in their ancestral homelands.

tree_branches.text:
A little further up the mighty Clarence River, a new civic hall is being built at Maclean, which will be incredible for the area. It will include a 290-seat auditorium, a function room, a modern stage and backstage area, a cafe-style food and beverage outlet, and dedicated car parking. Of course, all these amenities will be fully accessible. This was also made possible by funding from the previous Government, with the council also contributing some funds. The $10 million Yamba Road betterment project is still under construction, which was funded by the former Government following the 2022 floods. This is a great project because it lifts the height of Yamba Road, ensuring it will remain open for longer during flooding. I welcome this week's announcement by the Federal Government of funding for a similar project on Iluka Road at the Esk River. Lastly, the remarkable new Clarence Regional Aquatic Centre has been open for a few months, attracting 70,000 visitors over the winter months, which is quite remarkable. Thanks to funding from the Federal Government, a brand-new water slide will open in the coming weeks. I think there are actually two slides there. One is 75 metres in length and the other is 85 metres in length.

Mr Steve Whan: I hope you're the first one on it.

Mr RICHIE WILLIAMSON: That reminds me of an episode of The Simpsons , when Homer got stuck in a water slide. So no, I will not be the first one on it, Steve. But others will be lined up to get on. I know the entire Clarence community will treasure this new centre. Like every electorate, Clarence has had its ups and downs. Temporary Speaker Barr, you have been in the chair a number of times when I have mentioned the biosecurity issue of white spot in prawns. Sadly, but respectfully, I have to say that the Government has dropped the ball. The current white spot biosecurity order will end on 9 December, yet the Minister has given fishing families no plan for getting back to work. They have no idea what will happen on 10 December. I urge the Minister to speak with fishing families in the Clarence community to outline the Government's plan.

Tragically, I report to the House that in the past 12 weeks the Clarence Valley has seen three alleged murders that have rocked the community. The police are doing a terrific job, but my electorate has seen a serious spike in crime. I will work with the Government, the police, the community—anybody—to ensure that those statistics go down. Despite its size, Clarence is not a highly populated electorate, so to see three alleged murders in the past few months is uncharacteristic. That was the second and final instalment of Richie's year in review. I thank the House.

tree_branches.text:
I give a shout-out to the winners of Pink Up Berry's residents of the year prize. This year the town has already raised an outstanding $108,000. I also gave a community recognition statement about the Kiama Ultra Challenge. This gruelling endurance rowing event brought together 12 teams to back up the wonderful Nardia to row for the entire day. Not a single moment was missed, as local athletes showcased their determination and resilience. Some non‑athletes also took to the seat to take part and keep up with local heroes to raise much-needed funds for four different charities.

I recognise Homestead of Hope, which this year held a beautiful Melbourne Cup luncheon to raise funds to provide free meals, emergency accommodation and friendship in the wider community. Lastly, on Saturday, the fabulous Bondi2Berry Ride for Dementia Australia notched up its remarkable tenth year. The ride has become a cornerstone community event that combines a physical challenge with meaningful purpose. Cyclists rode 155 kilometres from Bondi to Berry along the State's scenic coastline, taking in the beautiful views, to raise crucial funds and awareness for dementia research and support services. This year the almost 200 participants raised more than $110,000 for dementia research. They knocked it out of the park. Locals turned out in droves at the Pit Stop in Kiama to welcome the riders and then again to celebrate them finishing in the town of Berry.

I congratulate Nick Young and the organising committee on this fabulous event. I thank the generous sponsors of those community events—businesses that dig deep into their pockets to ensure that funds are raised and community events are supported. I give a shout-out to them. It is week 44 of the Sunday Community Support Group, which gathers in Nowra every Sunday to hand out donations of food, clothing and toiletries. They will do that right through to the end of the year. I give a big shout-out to Kerry Fahey of Kerry's Klothes Kiama, Margie Tweedie at Care Essentials, IGA Berry and everybody else who generously donates to that group every week.

No round-up of our electorate's brilliant community spirit would be complete without the i98FM Illawarra Convoy. Now in its twenty-first year, the convoy delivered an absolutely triumphant result. It raised an incredible total of $2.3 million. That is just a fraction of the $30 million that the Illawarra Convoy has raised over the past two decades. It is an incredible event where a convoy of trucks, motorbikes and cars gather at the top end of our electorate and then over a few hours drive the back way down to Shellharbour Airport, where they marshal for a family fun day. More importantly, businesses compete every year to raise the most funds and be the lead truck. This year Ross Transport led the convoy, because they raised $305,000. More incredibly, thousands of people set up their camp chairs and eskies all the way down the route to cheer on the incredible convoy. I cannot wait for next year. I congratulate every single person in the electorate who donated, showed up or helped to organise that display of community spirit. I feel incredibly privileged to be representing our community in this place.

tree_branches.name: Ms KATELIN McINERNEY
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Kiama Electorate Fundraising Events > Ms KATELIN McINERNEY
tree_branches.text: Ms KATELIN McINERNEY ( Ki ama ) —I would like to recognise Mark Burns, the founder of The Man Walk, for his outstanding contribution to men's health and wellbeing in our community and across Australia. Beginning in Kiama in 2019, Mark launched a simple idea with powerful intent: to create a space where men could walk, talk, and support one another without judgement. Since then, The Man Walk has grown to over 80 locations nationwide, with more than 130,000 men taking part. Through Mark's leadership, thousands of men have found connection, routine, mateship, and a safe place to speak openly about the challenges they face. Countless participants credit The Man Walk with improving their mental health, building lasting friendships, and, in some cases, changing or even saving lives. Mark's vision has sparked a movement rooted in compassion and community strength. We thank him for walking alongside so many and for inspiring a culture of reaching out for support.

tree_branches.name: Hawkesbury Electorate
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Hawkesbury Electorate
tree_branches.text:
TEMPORARY SPEAKER ( Mr Clayton Barr ): Merry Christmas to you too.

Ms ROBYN PRESTON: I speak about several momentous occasions that occurred recently within the Hawkesbury electorate. Known for its proud heritage and encompassing historic towns such as Windsor, St Albans, Richmond, Ebenezer and Wilberforce—to name a few—Hawkesbury is a special place to live in, visit and learn about. I am privileged to be the member for the electorate, and I thoroughly enjoy occasions when we reach and celebrate significant anniversaries and milestones in our community. This week the restored Thomas James Bridge was officially opened, and the event was an example of that great public pride and celebration. Located on Settlers Road at Wisemans Ferry, the bridge has played a crucial role in connecting regions of the Hawkesbury since its construction in 1830. The Thomas James Bridge holds the prestigious title of the oldest in‑use bridge on mainland Australia—a source of great pride for Hawkesbury communities.

Unfortunately, recent flooding severely compromised the area around the bridge, resulting in major landslips and impacting the safe use of the bridge for residents. Funding from the State and Federal governments' recovery program enabled reconstruction of the bridge, with local contractor Delaney Civil appointed to complete the project. I note that the member for Gosford is in the Chamber. She participated in the conversations that followed the tragedy on our shared boundary, as both councils reached out to us for support. Stages of preliminary site assessment, bridge reconstruction and adjacent rock face stabilisation were critical steps in achieving restoration of the site.

Admirably, huge efforts were made during the repairs. The 181 original sandstone blocks, quarried from the surrounding hillside in 1830 to build the bridge, were carefully removed from the site. The beautiful sandstone blocks, originally cut and moved by hand, were meticulously replaced in exactly the same position to honour and replicate the original bridge as much as possible. It is remarkable that it could be mirrored 195 years later. I was incredibly honoured to attend the reopening of the Thomas James Bridge and celebrate the efforts and achievements of the project. I congratulate contractors Civil Delaney, Hawkesbury City Council, Central Coast Council, Macdonald Valley Association and the community groups on their collaboration and perseverance in completing the project. A great sense of pride, accomplishment and connectedness to heritage was shared amongst attendees at the event.

On a similar note, I recently attended another momentous occasion in the Hawkesbury electorate. I joined students, staff and members of the community at Macdonald Valley Public School to acknowledge and celebrate the school's 180th anniversary. Current and former students came together to reflect on the school's long history and unique place in the heart of the valley. Carrying the distinction of being one of the oldest government schools in New South Wales, Macdonald Valley Public School inspires a strong sense of pride and connection among the students, which was very special to witness.

Principal Sarah Allen and the dedicated staff possess a clear passion for supporting their 13 students, ensuring their time at school is spent making strong friendships, partaking in meaningful learning engagements and connecting with the community. The celebration was a very special occasion that highlighted the projects and achievements of the students, who are clearly well supported, inspired and connected to their learning. I congratulate the students, staff and community of Macdonald Valley Public School on reaching that milestone, and I look forward to hearing about their future endeavours. I also recognise and congratulate Uncle Cole, who gave us a wonderful welcome to country and smoking ceremony on the day.

Our region continues to experience the pressures and pace of a changing world, but it is grounding to come together in moments that remind us of who we are, where we have come from and what binds our communities together. Those milestones highlight the strength that comes from honouring our heritage while looking confidently towards the future. Whether it is safeguarding our historic infrastructure or nurturing the next generation of learners, the Hawkesbury continues to show that progress and tradition are not opposing forces but partners in reshaping a thriving and connected community. I am deeply proud to represent an electorate where local history is cherished, community spirit is strong and our shared story continues to grow richer over time.

tree_branches.name: North-West Sydney Housing Development
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > North-West Sydney Housing Development
tree_branches.text:
Additionally, the rezonings provide the corridors for the road connections of Bandon Road, Garfield Road West and Townsend Road. To understand the significance of those precincts, it is important to understand how we got to this point. In May 2017 the North West Priority Growth Area Land Use and Infrastructure Implementation Plan was released. It stated:

When fully developed, the North West Priority Growth Area will accommodate approximately 90,000 homes, 20,000 more than were forecast in 2006.

The implementation plan set out to facilitate the supply of 18,000 new homes by 2021 and 33,000 new homes by 2026, with the remaining 57,000 homes to be built by 2036. It highlighted the need to balance the needs of a growing population with opportunities for employment and recreation by establishing minimum and maximum residential densities as a priority, in line with infrastructure provisions.

By the time I was elected, almost all of the rezoning for residential use had been completed, creating a pipeline of new housing developments that extended to 2036. A significant amount of development was underway, set to peak in 2027, but the precincts needed to create jobs and green space languished. The new homes were built, but employment opportunities, recreation space and infrastructure provision were ignored—so much so that around 84 per cent of workers living in the Riverstone electorate are forced to leave the area to get to their place of employment, due to a lack of local job infrastructure. We have the most youth and young families in New South Wales, but one of the largest green space deficits. Necessary infrastructure like schools, roads and public transport simply did not keep pace with the population growth. That is what our Government inherited, why I entered Parliament and what I am determined to fix.

In the case of Marsden Park North and West Schofields, the precincts plans were first put on public exhibition in 2018 proposing a combined 11,000 new homes. At the time I was vice-president of the North West Business Chamber and strongly opposed the plans because of the amount of homes being proposed in an area known to be flood prone. Flood studies from 2020 and 2022 also expressed concerns about the number of homes being proposed. Both precincts were put on hold pending the outcome of flood evacuation modelling [FEM], which was delivered to Government in late 2022 and released to the public in 2023. The FEM report found that if development was allowed to proceed under those plans, around 5,000 people could become trapped in a major flood event. Those unworkable precinct plans left landholders in a state of limbo with no pathway forward.

Our Government had little choice but to scrap the original proposals and come up with new plans, which caused a lot of anger and confusion for affected landholders but was necessary to deliver a workable solution. Starting from scratch created the opportunity to devise a plan that provided a framework for what was really needed—jobs, green space and the road infrastructure necessary to help unlock the region. In stark contrast to the former Liberal Government, which pursued rezonings for thousands of new homes with no ability to have them approved and little regard for the need to supplement housing with jobs, the Minns Labor Government listened to experts, council, emergency services and, most importantly, the community. We understand that development needs more than just housing to create communities.

We are investing in the infrastructure that our area needs, with upgrades to roads like Bandon Road, Garfield Road East, Garfield Road West and Townson Road, as well as the Richmond Road upgrade between the M7 and Townson Road. There are nine new schools and many more being upgraded from Box Hill in the east to Marsden Park in the west. We have added over 160 new buses. The final business case for the Tallawong to St Marys metro is expected early next year. Those are not future promises; they are already underway. I note that West Schofields and Marsden Park North are not in the Riverstone electorate, but I have been working with the planning Minister since being elected to Parliament because they are part of my community and have a profound effect on my constituents. I say to the residents of Riverstone, Marsden Park North and West Schofields that their needs have been prioritised. After years of being told to wait, an achievable plan for the future is being proposed. I urge all residents to make a submission via the Planning Portal during the public exhibition period of these plans to make sure their voices are heard so that we can get the possible outcome for our area into the future.

tree_branches.name: Brookvale Public School
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Brookvale Public School
tree_branches.text:
For over a year, the Brookvale P&C has raised legitimate concerns about high school catchment boundaries. Currently, Brookvale Public School falls in the catchment area for the Northern Beaches Secondary College Cromer Campus without access to local single sex school options. The department has said that will continue, even though the nearby Northern Beaches Secondary College Freshwater Senior Campus is transitioning to a comprehensive years 7 to 12 high school from 2027 and the new Forest High School is opening in Allambie Height, the suburb right next door. The clear request from the Brookvale P&C is to include Brookvale in the intake area for the new years 7 to 12 Freshwater campus. I am also keen to see maximum choice for Brookvale families, including opening up Forest High School, Mackellar Girls Campus and Balgowlah Boys' Campus.

There are several reasons why keeping Brookvale zoned to Cromer campus is illogical and including it in the Freshwater catchment makes a lot more sense. Firstly, is geographic accessibility: Freshwater campus will be the closest high school, just 1.4 kilometres away from Brookvale Public School. It is mostly flat and a walkable or rideable distance from home for many Brookvale students. Cromer campus is much further away, involving a longer and more complex commute of up to 45 minutes, including multiple bus transfers. Over six years of high school that is about 1,800 hours commuting, equivalent to almost a full school year spent just travelling.

Secondly, is about maintaining community connectedness. Listening to the parent body at Brookvale, the reality is their networks of sports and social activities are the same as the families who will attend the Freshwater campus. Brookvale children train and play with Brookvale Football Club in Manly, play netball at Curl Curl, or are members of Surf Life Saving clubs at Freshwater and Curl Curl, among countless other engagements. We need to encourage continuity and depth of social connection, for both parents and students, across different parts of their lives. Thirdly, and very importantly, there is a fairness, equity and inclusion dimension to this issue. The position statement from Brookvale P&C states:

The decision to exclude Brookvale from the Freshwater Campus intake also appears to deepen class-based inequalities in the Northern Beaches public school system. Brookvale is home to a far more diverse mix of ethnic, cultural, and socio-economic backgrounds than many surrounding suburbs. Yet, we are being cut off from the high school options being made available to wealthier areas like Freshwater, Curl Curl, Manly and Balgowlah.

Brookvale students and families should get the same choices and opportunities as surrounding suburbs. Brookvale is a small school, so we are talking about a low number of students each year, which will have minimal impact on numbers at the Freshwater campus. The Brookvale Public School community feels that, in both process and outcome, the current high school zoning decision is unjustified and unfair. Frankly, I agree with them. I will not go into the details, but I think the Department of Education could have been more responsive and transparent on this issue.

I thank the members of the P&C, particularly president Hina Osmany, for being so engaged, eloquent and persistent in their advocacy. Brookvale is a small school doing great things. It needs to be celebrated, maintained and supported, not undermined. I have made clear to the education Minister's office my strong view that Brookvale primary students should be zoned for Freshwater campus from day one in 2027. Depending on capacity, I also think Brookvale students should have the option of Forest High, Mackellar Girls or Balgowlah Boys. Mr MICHAEL REGAN ( Wakehurst ) ( 17:41 :35 ): Brookvale Public School is the fifth smallest school on the northern beaches, with around 310 students enrolled in 2025. However, it may be small in numbers but it is bursting with spirit. The tight‑knit school is a place of social connection, belonging and purpose. The dedicated staff nurture every child, supporting them to flourish. The school has a rich program of extracurricular activities and also supports academic excellence, hosting an opportunity class since the beginning of this year. The thriving school culture is testament to the commitment of all the teachers, mums and dad, and the great kids at the school. Tonight I acknowledge and thank the entire school community, particularly principal Mr Luke Richmond for his excellent leadership. Brookvale is one of many excellent public schools in my electorate of Wakehurst, but right now it is facing some unique pressures.

For over a year, the Brookvale P&C has raised legitimate concerns about high school catchment boundaries. Currently, Brookvale Public School falls in the catchment area for the Northern Beaches Secondary College Cromer Campus without access to local single sex school options. The department has said that will continue, even though the nearby Northern Beaches Secondary College Freshwater Senior Campus is transitioning to a comprehensive years 7 to 12 high school from 2027 and the new Forest High School is opening in Allambie Height, the suburb right next door. The clear request from the Brookvale P&C is to include Brookvale in the intake area for the new years 7 to 12 Freshwater campus. I am also keen to see maximum choice for Brookvale families, including opening up Forest High School, Mackellar Girls Campus and Balgowlah Boys' Campus.

There are several reasons why keeping Brookvale zoned to Cromer campus is illogical and including it in the Freshwater catchment makes a lot more sense. Firstly, is geographic accessibility: Freshwater campus will be the closest high school, just 1.4 kilometres away from Brookvale Public School. It is mostly flat and a walkable or rideable distance from home for many Brookvale students. The decision to exclude Brookvale from the Freshwater Campus intake also appears to deepen class-based inequalities in the Northern Beaches public school system. tree_branches.name: East Hills Electorate
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > East Hills Electorate
tree_branches.text:
Our churches play an equally important role. We are fortunate to have many active congregations across our electorate, each running their own internal Christmas donation drives. These groups quietly collect food, gifts and supplies to ensure that families doing it tough feel supported. Organisations like Georges River Life Care continue their year-round support. This year it is again running its "light, hope, joy, strength" Christmas appeal. This provides practical help and emotional support to people who need it most. Another inspiring example of East Hills community spirit is the partnership between Picnic Point High School and Keith's Closet. The Picnic Point High School community came together to deliver more than 30 boxes filled with toiletries and accessories for people accessing mental health services. Every item was thoughtfully wrapped, a simple gesture that will make someone's Christmas a little brighter. The community even dedicated a full day to packing, giving students and families a hands-on opportunity to support others. Keith's Closet's Christmas drives and annual Shoebox Appeal are now in their fifth year. The organisation is aiming for 1,000 boxes and is well on its way. Its work has brought comfort and hope to countless people across Sydney and the East Hills electorate.

Our businesses are also stepping up. The Canterbury Bankstown Chamber of Commerce is running its annual Christmas toy drive, bringing the local business community together to give every child the chance to feel the joy of the season. The efforts of the chamber and local businesses show how strongly our small business owners care for the families they serve. It is such a privilege to be able to deliver these toys to sick kids at our local hospital, bringing a small bit of joy to those facing some of the toughest moments of their young lives. Groups like Anglicare, through initiatives such as Toys 'n' Tucker, continue to support local households with food and presents, making sure Christmas can be a time of celebration, not stress.

We also see this community spirit shine through in our local Christmas carols. Panania Anglican Church is once again hosting their Christmas carols event, bringing together families, neighbours and parish members to celebrate the season in song. Over at Rotary Club of Padstow, they are preparing for their much-loved Carols by Candlelight. This family event continues to draw a huge crowd every year. It has become one of the biggest and most anticipated community gatherings. It lights up the season and gives families a chance to come together in a joyful and meaningful way.

All of these examples show that the East Hills electorate is built on generosity, community and genuine care for others. This spirit is not limited to one organisation or one suburb. It is seen throughout Panania, Revesby, Padstow, East Hills, Condell Park, Georges Hall and every corner of our electorate. I am delighted to formally acknowledge my own Christmas card competition winner, Timothy Zhang, from Panania North Public School. His beautiful Christmas design, including a very Aussie Santa, will be in letterboxes throughout our community very soon.

As we move towards the end of the year, I acknowledge every volunteer, every school, every community organisation or group, every business, every faith organisation, and every family who has contributed to these efforts. They are the reason East Hills remains such a strong, supportive and deeply connected community. To everyone who has given their time, their donations, or simply a moment of kindness, I say thank you for making our electorate a great place to live, and reminding us what community means. I wish everyone a safe and happy holiday season, spent with family and friends, or the person that cares for them most.
